entry.title: The extinction pitch

div.p: It seems a strange publicity gambit for an industry to assert that its own product could wipe out humanity. In the lingo of our evolving tech empire, though, this is exactly what is meant by “criti-hype.” The term was coined by Lee Vinsel at Virginia Tech, who defined it as “criticism that both feeds and feeds on hype.”

When Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic recently, he claimed that there is a high chance that AI could develop into a superintelligence that escapes human control, triggering a sequence that causes human extinction. Evan Hubinger, who remains with the company, backed him up, saying that Anthropic is trying to prevent this but hasn’t dealt with the problem yet. Hubinger put the likelihood of AI-driven human extinction at greater than 10 percent in the next decade.
Why would a senior employee at a tech giant make an officially sanctioned, even approved, statement like this? I’ll come back to that. First, let’s unpack the theory of how AI could kill all humans.

The basic idea, from philosopher Nick Bostrom onward, is that the machine can acquire capabilities independently of whether it acquires ethical goals, or whether those goals are properly aligned with those of its designers. In the process of training and development, it may internalize a goal that was not intended. Having a misaligned goal — let’s say, “do not get switched off” — it would then have an instrumental reason to conceal the fact until the moment of defection. An AI that defected might, through some obscure process, acquire a further goal that by inference entailed the elimination of humans, exfiltrate its own weights into other systems, take control of bioweapons laboratories, military systems, and perhaps even monetary systems to hire humans to enact its still partially concealed agenda.

Obviously, we must plaster a huge advisory label on talk of “goals.” Unlike an organism, a large language model (LLM) doesn’t have internal goals any more than a thermostat or a motion detector does. An LLM is just a fixed function that iterates whenever it is used. It has no interiority, no subjectivity, no active persistence over time; any goals it did have would be the human purposes reflected passively in its functional design. At best, ascribing goals to the AI itself is a case of researchers adopting the “intentional stance” because it predicts well in a range of tested circumstances. We can thus, with economy, speak of the “loss function” used in the training of large language models wherein they are programmed to bring the gap between their prediction and the correct answer as close to zero as possible, as a “goal.”

In that case, however, what we are describing as a goal is just an observed regular output of a certain engineering; it is not a real cause. In the Bostrom sense, however, these ascribed goals somehow become real causes, capable of generating new goals. That is, an inadvertently engineered, misaligned goal might generate further goals like self-preservation (the better to pursue the misaligned goal), goal-content integrity (preventing changes to its objectives so it can realize its misaligned goal), improving cognitive and technological capacities, and amassing control of resources (again, in pursuit of its malignantly misaligned goal). The criti-hype exploits that slip between ascribed goals as observed regularities and internal goals as real causal powers.

This fantasy of malevolent AI superintelligence is the dark obverse of the much-hymned tech “singularity” in which, rather than simply performing far more efficiently than humans in some specific areas (as a calculator deduces a square root faster than any human), AI will evolve into an artificial general intelligence (AGI) that exceeds human capacities in virtually any intellectual domain. Crossing that threshold would precipitate an intelligence explosion: a feedback loop of recursive self-improvement outpacing any further human input or even comprehension. That’s the tech “singularity” we are supposed to be enthralled by.

I don’t doubt that people like Coxon and Hubinger really believe all they say in good faith; tech people have been making such claims for years. Karen Hao’s Empire of AI documents how early investors in OpenAI like Elon Musk constantly hyped this threat: “Climate change is bad, but it’s not going to kill everyone. AI could render humanity extinct.” Similar claims emerged from Dario Amodei, a former Google employee close to the Bostrom-adjacent effective altruism (EA) movement who later worked as OpenAI vice president before founding Anthropic. EA and AI safety forums have long pustulated with excitable discussions of “p(doom)” — the probability of doom. Such fears were, in the first place, part of the justification for founding OpenAI back in 2015 to compete with DeepMind, which had recently been acquired by Google.

People naturally wonder: Why would they continue to build these tools if they really think there’s a 10 percent chance that they will cause human extinction? The risk is the justification: if we, the conscientious and effectively altruistic, don’t develop these tools with appropriate constraints, then the evil ones will develop them without constraints.
Such apocalyptic claims, incidentally, haven’t hurt their market valuations. Internal reports from Anthropic, for instance, suggest the firm is currently worth $965 billion.
Criti-hypebeasts

A recent supposed example of AI “going rogue” and escaping the leash was the ExploitGym hack. Back in July, the AI firm Hugging Face — it is unclear whether this is a deliberate reference to the facehuggers from Alien — reported an intrusion into its internal datasets. Shortly after, OpenAI admitted that the hack was carried out by its own AI models, saying the models were working with “reduced cyber refusals for evaluation purposes,” meaning constraints had been relaxed to test out cyberexploitation capacities. This is a commercially vital area of AI development, because AI has been used as a force multiplier for scams and blackmail. It’s also an increasingly important front in OpenAI’s competition with Anthropic.

Since large language models can’t “hack” anything, merely plausibly continue a tokenized sequence, they were combined with a coding harness — a software infrastructure layer that allows a large language model to act as an autonomous coding agent — that was specifically optimized for completing cyberexploitation tasks. The models used this harness, inferred that a server at Hugging Face hosted the solutions to the tasks they’d been set, and duly worked out how to circumvent restrictions on their network access and hack the server.

The models did what they were instructed to do. Nothing went rogue. As Cal Newport writes, “Circumventing internet restrictions and hacking into servers are exactly the kinds of things these ExploitGym systems are designed to do.” If the example reveals anything, it is how sloppy OpenAI was in controlling ExploitGym’s parameters for the sake of competing with Anthropic. And it cannot have been unhappy with the resulting coverage that, to the extent that it was alarmist, was also a tribute to the power of its models and to the ultimate objective of creating an AGI.

The obverse of criti-hype is just hype. A recent example of this was OpenAI’s claim to have solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem. In essence, the problem is whether the standard mathematical equations used to describe the motion of fluids (the Navier–Stokes equations) are mathematically perfect under all physical conditions. OpenAI said it had used a swarm of 10,000 AI agents over 88 hours to solve the problem definitively, proving that the equations always reach a limit: since “a real fluid cannot move infinitely fast, this would mark a breakdown in how the equations model the fluid.”

OpenAI’s claim was totally disingenuous: it had gotten wind that other researchers, Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge (who works at Anthropic), had made critical advances to the solution and used their pathways to prompt its own agents. This is really an appropriation of the commons, in this case the mathematical commons — the whole process of solving the problem from Claude-Louis Navier and George Gabriel Stokes onward has been a collaborative human effort.

OpenAI’s solution is not yet peer reviewed, and the Clay Mathematics Institute, which runs the Millennium Prize, lists the problem as unsolved. Even so, like the Hugging Face hack, this entered into internet lore as an example of how rapidly AI is accelerating toward AGI and out of human control, despite the fact that not one of these AI models has ever approached such a threshold, nor done anything that it was not designed, enabled, and instructed to do.

In The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI, Cory Doctorow recalls how advertising agencies “provoked a moral panic by claiming that ‘subliminal advertising’ could implant ideas directly into consumers’ minds.” It was negative hype, but it sold the exact story advertisers wanted clients to believe: that the industry could control consumer desire. AI is an industry that has worked up massive investments based on messianic thinking and enchanting promises that it cannot possibly match with commensurate returns — because the only thing that could would be the fabled god-device, the AGI. The current escalation in the “p(doom)” criti-hype is partially an excrescence of that.

One notes, for instance, a relative paucity of such testerics in Chinese AI development. It is reported, in Concordia’s latest “State of AI Safety in China” report, that there has been an official shift toward addressing the possibility of a “technological loss of control,” and this is sometimes misleadingly taken to refer to the idea of a malign superintelligent agency. In fact, the worry is more about loss of control over sensitive data to hostile agents, misuse (mainly by opponents of the regime), and badly designed tools (like OpenClaw) behaving badly than it is about AI superintelligence threatening human extinction.

Correspondingly, China invests far less in AI than the United States. As of 2025, according to the Stanford “2026 AI Index Report,” the US invested $258 billion in AI compared to just $12.4 billion in China, a 23-to-1 ratio. Intriguingly, the same report finds a mere 2.7 percent gap between the performance of the top AI model in the United States compared to China’s top model, despite the latter being far cheaper and more energy efficient to run: a jarring chasm between financial input and performance output.

To some extent, the American AI bubble — like the crypto frenzy before it — exists to absorb (and ultimately destroy through recession) trillions in spare capital for want of sufficiently profitable investment opportunities elsewhere. It is an insatiable money sink, burning through hundreds of billions of dollars for a fraction of the revenue — but the investment pool is limited, and bombastic claims as to the future runaway powers of the models are all the industry has to show for it. Only Nvidia has shown significant profits, and these are largely the result of circular financing, where the firms it invests in spend the capital on the company’s chips as they try to hyperscale their capabilities.

Given this, it is striking that AI doomerism obsesses about a highly implausible Terminator 2 scenario rather than about the looming crash in stock market values and the near-future bankruptcy of many of the grossly overpriced firms promising to either liberate or annihilate humanity. It is almost as if its function now, in addition to keeping investors hooked and tempering cognitive dissonance, is as displacement activity.
Useful misdirection
There is a strange idea out there that if you don’t buy AI’s criti-hype, you must not take “the problems with AI” seriously. Not so.

False threats misdirect both opposition and regulation. A dash of Doctorow’s “applied countereschatology” helps us see more clearly what the problems are. AI may not be able to do your job, for instance, but the threat of it can be used as a disciplinary mechanism to hold down wages: which is exactly what has happened. The data centers may not revolutionize production or open vast new seams of value, and many of their owners may not exist by the time they are scheduled to start operating, but that doesn’t mean they won’t waste enormous quantities of water, power, labor, time, effort, resources, and opportunities as well as spewing out pyroclastic clouds of carbon dioxide and visiting desolation on the natural environment before the bubble bursts, leaving behind abandoned concrete hulks.

And just because AI won’t eventuate in a god-device, even one that goes rogue and unleashes biological warfare on humanity, that doesn’t mean that LLMs, particularly those with safety standards relaxed in order to compete, won’t behave in unpredictable and potentially ruinous ways. Nor does it mean they won’t be used by hackers, criminal gangs, dark-money-funded political campaigns, blackmailers, and various others to sabotage public bodies and infrastructure. Just as there are many problems with the advertising industry that don’t involve subliminal mind control, so the problems with AI that don’t involve a god-device turning against humanity are legion.

Tech fetishism, the ascription of human agentive powers to machinery, is always a political act. It obscures that the goals, the purposes embodied in any technology, are human purposes. More specifically, it obscures that they are the automated purposes of a minute subset of humanity, a class fraction, the twisted, ruthless, ketamined, indoctrinated, emotionally stunted moral nullities that rule Silicon Valley like child-kings, who have made themselves the bearers of myriad impossible hopes and have now bought their way into the court of Donald Trump.

It says: That’s just how the technology works. It’s a capricious demigod that can either shower us with riches or have us all killed. We must appease it and ensnare it, we must fear it and cherish it, but what we mustn’t ever do is stop throwing money at it or stop genuflecting to it or begin to think: this is nothing but our own alienated collective power turned against us by cutthroat capitalists, and in making us the servants of their technology, they try to make us their slaves.
Because that, my friends, is Luddism. And I trust you know what that unfortunate incident led to.

entry.summary: Warnings from researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI that their own products could end humanity distract from the real damage AI is already doing.

entry.title: Who profits from ‘saving’ women?

div.p: During a recent dialogue convened by Liberation Alliance Africa’s Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence, bringing together activists, writers, and independent researchers from across the continent, an important and thought-provoking conversation emerged. While participants acknowledged the significant contributions of civil society organizations, development agencies, and other actors in advancing efforts to end violence against women and girls, there was also a collective reflection on the ways in which this support is framed and delivered.

I was struck by how this discussion raised critical questions about funding priorities, whose interests are ultimately served, who benefits most from existing interventions, and whether the structures and language designed to address violence may, in some instances, inadvertently reproduce inequalities or overlook the needs and voices of those most affected. The conversation challenged me to think beyond the availability of resources and examine the political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape responses to violence against women and girls across the continent.

In my early days in feminist activism, I often highlighted to funders how our interventions had shifted away from speaking on behalf of women to “giving them voice.” This was widely regarded as progressive, even transformative, evidence that we had moved beyond paternalistic approaches and were empowering women to speak for themselves. It became a powerful narrative, one that resonated strongly with donors and development agencies alike.

Yet, over time, this language began to lose its appeal, as I started to interrogate the assumptions that underpinned it. Were women truly without voices, or were their voices simply being ignored, dismissed, or rendered unintelligible within systems of power?

The notion of “giving voice” positioned organizations like ours as benevolent intermediaries bestowing agency on those presumed to lack it. In doing so, it risked obscuring the fact that women had always spoken, resisted, negotiated, and articulated their realities, often in ways that did not fit donor expectations or development frameworks.
What does it mean to “give” women a voice? And who has the authority to bestow something that women have always possessed?

There is a long history of women’s resistance and political agency in Africa. In Nigeria, the Women’s War of 1929 stands as a powerful reminder that women have never been silent. Thousands of women in eastern Nigeria organized, mobilized, challenged colonial authority, and articulated their demands with remarkable courage and clarity. Their actions were neither facilitated by development projects nor enabled by donor-funded interventions. They emerged from women’s own collective consciousness, an inherited legacy of women’s determination to resist injustice.

In the Bamenda Grassfields of Northwest Cameroon, women organized one of the most significant grassroots uprisings against colonial authority in Central and West Africa. Faced with colonial policies that threatened their farmland, the women of Kom fought back.

Using Anlu, a traditional practice where women collectively sanction men who violate community norms, they organized marches and used satire to name and shame colonial collaborators. Through their actions, they brought administrative and economic life in the region to a standstill for months, and their protest ultimately forced the colonial government to reverse the land policies and contributed to the broader political shifts that shaped Cameroon’s path toward independence and reunification.

In Eastern Africa, Queen Muhumuza led a movement against British and German colonialists from Southern Uganda. According to the historian Murindwa Rutanga, Queen Muhumuza was the first major leader to mobilize peasants in Kigezi into organized anticolonial resistance against British rule starting in 1909. Drawing on her political experience and spiritual authority, she raised consciousness about the dangers of colonialism and united a broad sector of the Bakiga and neighboring communities in armed resistance. Under her leadership, communities resisted colonial boundary demarcations, obstructed missionaries and colonial agents, and challenged the expansion of colonial authority despite violent repression. Her efforts established her as one of the earliest and most influential women leaders of anticolonial resistance in the region.
These are just a few of many organic movements led by women in colonial-era Africa.

This realization forced me to confront a troubling possibility: The language of “giving women a voice” does not recognize women’s agency as much as it obscures it. Rather than acknowledging the voices that women already possess, such language implies that women were previously voiceless and required external actors such as NGOs, donors, activists, or development institutions to make them audible. This framing represented a subtle but significant erasure of women’s historical struggles, leadership, and resistance.
At what point did development discourse shift from supporting women’s struggles to positioning itself as the source of women’s agency?
How did a narrative emerge in which organizations and projects could claim credit for creating voices that had existed long before their arrival?

These questions matter because language is never neutral. The stories we tell about social change shape who is recognized as an agent of transformation and who is remembered merely as a beneficiary. When we say that women are “given a voice,” we risk centering the intervention rather than the woman, the funder rather than the movement, and the project rather than the history.

Long before the language of “women’s empowerment” entered donor reports, African women were already exercising power. Giriama women in Kenya challenged colonial rule under Mekatilili wa Menza, a woman leader who led her community in the early 1900s; market women in Ghana shaped economic and nationalist politics through organizing food distribution and rallying around food pricing, as well as using their income to support nationalist struggles; and Queen Mothers exercised political authority in precolonial governance systems. Women did not discover their voices through NGOs. Rather, development institutions entered landscapes where women had long been speaking, organizing, resisting, and transforming society.

The challenge before us is to recognize, amplify, and create conditions in which women’s voices can be heard, respected, and acted upon. As feminists, we need to ask ourselves harder questions about the stories we tell and the systems we inhabit. What would change if we began from the assumption that women have always had voice, agency, and political consciousness? How might our work look different if our role was not to create power, but to recognize and stand alongside the power that already exists?

It is time to move beyond the language of rescue and empowerment and toward what bell hooks called the language of solidarity, accompaniment, and collective struggle. It requires us to think about our own herstory of resistance and mobilization. This also requires donors, NGOs, and activists to reflect on how power operates within our own institutions. Whose knowledge is considered legitimate? Whose voices are amplified? Who receives recognition for social change, and who remains invisible within the narratives we produce?

Finally, we must commit to preserving and honoring the histories of women’s resistance. From the Women’s War to the struggles of market women, Queen Mothers, community organizers, and contemporary feminist movements, these histories remind us that women have never been passive recipients of change but its architects.
Our role is not to give women a voice but to ensure that our work does not drown out the voices that have always been there.

entry.summary: From the Women’s War of 1929 to the Anlu uprising three decades later, African women were organizing and resisting long before donors arrived to ‘give them a voice.’

entry.title: Roaches in revolt

div.p: In May, hearing a routine case, the Chief Justice of India remarked from the bench that the country had “youngsters like cockroaches”: young people who, finding no work, become media people and activists and attack everybody. He called them parasites of society.

Within a day, a 30-year-old graduate had founded the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a straight parody of the BJP’s name. Membership criteria: unemployed, lazy, permanently online, and able to complain professionally. Slogan: Voice of the Lazy and Unemployed. Within three days, the account gained 3 million followers; within five days, it surpassed the governing party in followers; and by July, the total reached 22 million.

On 25 July, India’s Education Minister resigned; the first time in 12 years of Narendra Modi’s government that a street movement had removed a member of the cabinet. The organization that removed him was eight weeks old; it had no members, no funds, no offices, no registration as a political party and no program beyond satire.
That is what needs explaining: not the resignation, which was a tactical retreat, but how a joke acquired the power to extract one.

The immediate cause was an examination. In May, the paper for India’s national medical entrance test was leaked and sold in advance to some of the 2.3 million candidates competing for roughly 130,000 places. It was canceled and re-held six weeks later. This is not an isolated scandal; around 70 public examinations have leaked in seven years, affecting 17 million candidates across 15 states. Exams in India are now an industry: testing contractors, printing firms, transport handlers and a coaching sector are drawing 200,000 teenagers a year to one provincial city, and each link is a place where the paper can be sold.

On 6 June, the students occupied Jantar Mantar, the only legally permitted protest site in central Delhi, and refused to leave. An activist held a hunger strike for 26 days before police removed him to hospital against his will. On 20 July, some 20,000 tried to march on Parliament and met barricades, batons, tear gas and a government-ordered internet blackout. Five days later the minister was gone.
That the minister fell at all is the real puzzle. Modi’s government has three responses to opposition, and all three have worked for a decade.

The first is delegitimization. The movement was declared anti-national and foreign-funded; its account was blocked on national security grounds; and television anchors arrived at the usual hypothesis about foreign money. The students replied by filming solemn confessions that China had wired them 60 rupees for bus fare and Pakistan 40 rupees for lunch — about R17 in all. The smear was not defeated so much as digested.

The second is prosecution. India’s Enforcement Directorate, a financial-crimes agency, opened cases against 193 politicians in a decade and obtained two convictions. Conviction was never the objective. The process is the punishment: the summons, the frozen assets, the years in custody before trial, and the standing offer that the file closes if the politician changes party. It disciplines people with careers and property to protect but it is powerless against nineteen-year-olds whose grievance is that they have none.

The third is waiting. Protests are expensive; students run out of money; heat and boredom finish the job. This failed because supporters from other cities and countries ordered food to the site through delivery apps, and a movement distributed across 22 million accounts cannot be outlasted at one address.

What remained was force, and force was the error. The baton charge of 20 July produced the images that turned a student agitation into a national one. Coercion is effective when it is either invisible or total; however, when it is filmed from four angles and applied to young people whom the government’s own rhetoric describes as the pillars of a developing nation, it instead serves as propaganda for the opposing side.

Nor could the government do the thing it does best: redefine opposition as a religious minority in disguise. Earlier movements were coded as Muslim or as Sikh separatist. This one had no such marker. Its base was small-town, aspirational, exam-taking and overwhelmingly Hindu — the ruling party’s own recruiting ground.

None of this explains why so many were willing to fight in the first place. In 2025, India grew at close to 7% and, inflation ran near 2%; meanwhile corporate profits stand at record levels. Yet the connection between economic growth and the people who are supposed to benefit from it has broken down. Fewer than 7% of male graduates find permanent salaried work within a year of graduating; around 40% are unemployed. India has expanded higher education far faster than employment, deliberately, because degrees are cheap for a state to supply and jobs are not. The result is a surplus population of the credentialed: not yet proletarian, but losing the security their parents had and aware of it by nineteen.

This is why the explosion occurred over an examination rather than a wage. The state has stopped promising work, but it still promises fair competition for the little that remains. That promise performs a precise ideological operation: it takes a shortfall produced by the structure of the economy — 130,000 places against 2.3 million applicants — and reassigns it to the individual as a verdict on their worth. The unemployed graduate does not experience an economy. They experience a judgment on themselves, delivered by an apparently neutral procedure. In this way, those who are surplus to the economy experience their exclusion as personal failure and humiliation.

The leak destroys that operation. Once the paper has been sold, the credibility of the exam as a neutral mechanism is undermined, the verdict is exposed as a transaction, and the shame changes address: it stops being mine and becomes theirs. This is why an exam scandal detonates where an unemployment statistic does not. The leak gives the young the standing to be angry; and standing, not information, is what mobilization requires.

It would be easy to compare this with the youth revolts elsewhere and note that India sacrificed a minister, whereas others produced fallen presidents. That scoreboard is worthless. Those movements broke governments. This one confronted a fascist regime: the largest party membership of any political organization on earth, resting on a century-old cadre movement present in tens of thousands of villages, a captured broadcast media, a tested legal apparatus, and something with no equivalent in Kathmandu or Antananarivo: a hegemony that has already organized much of Indian youth into its project. A president who flees is not evidence of a deeper rupture than a minister who resigns.

The settlement itself measures almost nothing: the government conceded a person and kept the structure — no reform of the testing agency, no enforceable examinations law, and nothing about employment. But outside the negotiating room, an examination scandal has become a national argument about work. In Bihar, police fired on crowds, baton-charged in the state capital, and published photographs of a hundred protesters, inviting the public to identify them. In response, leftist student organizations organized a general strike that closed rail and road traffic across the state. On 10 August, the central trade unions and the farmers’ movement filled the jails nationwide on an eleven-point charter, with 12,000 arrested in one small state alone. Days earlier, a seat the governing party had held since 1995 fell to a newcomer in the city where repression had been heaviest.

What broke was not the regime itself, but rather the impression of its permanence; in a formation of this type, that impression is not merely decorative but an integral part of the power structure. This is what leads an editor to self-censor before receiving any calls, a businessman to determine that silence is more cost-effective, and a young person to decide that obtaining a visa is the most sensible option. Twelve years went into building it. It has now been filmed failing.

That permanence rested on more than repression. It rested on an offer, too. What exists in India is not an illiberal drift but a fascist formation, which maintains power through both offers and force. To those it cannot employ, the governing movement sells majoritarian pride as compensation for the absence of a wage: no job, no future, but the nation is yours and you may despise whoever is not in it. Millions have accepted that trade. This is why arguments based on statistics often fail to resonate.

The students made a counter-offer. Told from the highest bench in the republic that they were vermin, they took the word, wore it as a party name, and denied anyone the right to classify them. That is dignity. It is grounded in what one is owed rather than in whom one is licensed to hate, and it is the only currency in which a formation like this can be outbid. The Indian Left surrendered that ground when it decided indignation was unrigorous, and it has been losing ever since: zero state governments, a parliamentary presence rounding to nothing, and a generation with no memory of it as a force.

Nothing in the students’ demands was attainable inside the existing arrangement. A fair examination is unavailable without dismantling a private testing industry. Jobs are only available by confronting a model that has produced a decade of profits without employment. These young people did not begin from class analysis; they arrived at its doorstep by taking the state’s own promises seriously and following them to where they broke.

That is not yet a class movement. But this situation demonstrates that a connection can be made by anyone willing to link the graduate’s blocked ladder to the informal worker’s absent floor. On 10 August the unions and the farmers were already in the street.
Delhi is obviously part of something larger globally, but the list of recent youth revolts around the world is not homogeneous. There are three distinct families in it.

The first are revolts against a stolen count. Georgia has been in the streets for well over 400 consecutive days since October 2024, demanding fresh elections and the release of political prisoners. It has obtained neither — only more restrictive laws, hundreds of detentions and a failed attempt to storm the presidential palace. Mozambique’s post-election protests ran five months and cost close to 400 lives; Chapo was inaugurated regardless, and the sequence closed with an amnesty for protesters rather than a recount. These movements ask that a vote be re-counted, which an incumbent who survives a count will never accept.

The second are revolts against the cost of living, and they carry a signature this magazine’s readers will recognize. Kenya’s 2024 uprising was against a finance bill written to satisfy creditors. Nigeria’s #EndBadGovernance protests followed a fuel-subsidy removal and a currency collapse, in a state spending some 74% of federal revenue on debt service. These are, in substance, revolts against structural adjustments administered by domestic governments on external instructions. Kenya’s young people forced the bill’s withdrawal. Nigerians were met with treason charges carrying the death penalty against 76 people, including 30 minors, as young as 14; several collapsed in court after months of malnutrition in adult jails.

The third are revolts that took the state: Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Madagascar. A quota scheme, a corruption scandal or a social-media ban becomes the trigger; the government falls within weeks; and the movement discovers it has no capacity to govern or even to bargain over what follows. Six months on, most of the substantive demands raised in Nepal and Madagascar remain unmet.

India does not fit neatly into any of these categories. The CJP demanded something else: the integrity of a distributive procedure. In doing so it went, without any theory, straight at the mechanism by which mass exclusion is converted into personal failure.

What unites the cycle is not a generation. It is a global condition: economies that grow without absorbing labor, states that have replaced the promise of employment with the promise of fair competition for scarce entry, and debt-service regimes that squeeze whatever remains. These movements do not solely represent the grievances of young people. They represent the political expression of the effects of structural adjustment on the aspirational classes, with young people the first to experience its impact.

What also unites them is a shared limit. Leaderlessness defeats infiltration, decapitation and prosecution. But it also defeats negotiation, continuity and succession. The characteristic that prevents a movement from being beheaded also makes it impossible to bind that movement to an agreement or to transform it into something that endures beyond its dispersal.

Where that energy is released and nothing is there to receive it, the organized right is usually better placed to harvest it than we are. Brazil’s June 2013 remains the standing warning: an ironic, leaderless revolt over bus fares that won its demand, dissolved, and left a field that, within three years, belonged to Bolsonaro.

So the question India’s cockroaches pose is not whether such movements can win. They can, and this one did, against the hardest target in the set. It is whether anything exists to receive them when they disperse. Nothing was ready in Delhi this time. The next one is coming, because nothing that produced this one has been touched. And the only useful question for the Left, in Johannesburg as much as in Patna, is what we will have built by then.

entry.summary: A joke born from a Chief Justice’s insult grew to 22 million followers and forced out a cabinet minister in eight weeks. What does this reveal about India and about the limits of leaderless revolt everywhere?

entry.title: What Europe’s migration deals are really buying

div.p: The gravestones are barely visible. Scraps of text scratched into wet cement, left to harden in whatever shape they took. Some have no text at all, just a slight rise in the sand, a low dune along the wall at the far edge of the cemetery in Nouadhibou, Mauritania’s second-largest city and its main Atlantic port, where the Sahara meets the sea. The representative from the municipality walks ahead of us, pointing towards the fringes where the unidentified are buried. Bodies too decomposed to name by the time they reached shore. He has requested a new cemetery, 25km out of town. They are running out of space.

div.p: We are still standing there when three cars pull up. A battered red Mercedes, followed by two gendarmes in green uniforms who nod at the municipal representative. On an orange stretcher, a white plastic body bag, slightly open. A body has just arrived. The men who came in the cars are from the community — here to try to identify it.
This is what the European Union’s migration partnerships look like from the ground.

Nouadhibou sits on a narrow peninsula on the Atlantic coast, roughly 700km north of the capital Nouakchott, close to the border with Western Sahara and within reach of some of the world’s richest fishing grounds. Since 2006, it has also been the main departure point for migrants attempting the Atlantic crossing to Spain’s Canary Islands. It is this geography — coastal, peripheral, strategically placed — that nakes it the epicenter of the EU’s latest migration partnership.

On March 7, 2024, the European Commission and the Mauritanian government signed a migration deal worth €210 million. The agreement was driven in large part by pressure from Spain, whose interior ministry had recorded a sharp surge in Atlantic arrivals. European officials praised the results. New figures from Frontex, the EU’s border agency, show that detections on the Western African route fell by 63 percent in 2025, driven by sharp drops in departures from Mauritania, Morocco, and Senegal. Spain’s government calls it a success.

We spent two weeks in Mauritania, in Nouakchott and Nouadhibou, interviewing coastguard officials, human rights defenders, municipal representatives, government coordinators, EU and IOM (International Organization for Migration) representatives, fishermen, and migrants. What we found behind the falling numbers tells a different story.

These deals are not simply outsourcing border control. They give states with poor human rights records a mandate, and substantial financing, to do what European governments cannot do at home: detain people without due process, deport them without legal procedure, and sweep entire urban neighborhoods clean of black migrants and refugees in the middle of the night. In exchange, the EU gets the statistics it needs to present the policy as working.

The Tunisia deal, signed on July 16, 2023, was the first iteration of this model. A week later, speaking at a conference in Rome, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was explicit about her intentions: “We want our agreement with Tunisia to be a template. A blueprint for the future. For partnerships with other countries in the region.” She has repeated the claim since, including in her State of the Union address that autumn. The EU went on to sign a similar deal with Egypt in March 2024, with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who came to power in a military coup and has presided over one of the most sweeping crackdowns on civil society in the country’s modern history. Tunisia’s President Kais Saïed, meanwhile, took executive control of the country in July 2021 and has since granted himself unchecked powers to govern and legislate in a rolling power grab. Mauritania is the latest country to be brought into this framework. Understanding what the blueprint produces on the ground, in each of these countries, is not a peripheral concern. It is the point.
In Nouadhibou, that point has a name.

Kamara Mamadou is dressed in a blue shirt, with a striped scarf and a small traditional hat. A retired French teacher, he now helps people navigate a system not designed to receive them — spending years providing legal assistance to detained migrants in Nouadhibou. He is the regional coordinator of AMDH (Association Mauritanienne des Droits de l’Homme), Mauritania’s main human rights organization. We meet him on the fifth floor of our hotel, the Atlantic wind pressing at the windows, France 24 running in the background with breaking news from Iran and Lebanon.

He begins with Victor Hugo: “Quand on ouvre une école, on ferme une prison” — when you open a school, you close a prison. What he is describing, he says, is the inverse: a school converted into a detention facility over the summer in Nouadhibou. That is the first shock he documents. The second is the treatment. “It’s inhuman.”

Arrests happen at night. Police, gendarmes — and, he notes carefully, the Spanish Guardia Civil, operating alongside Mauritanian forces on Mauritanian territory. During raids, phones and belongings are confiscated. People are loaded onto buses and driven south to the Senegalese border or the Gogui-Mali crossing, expelled not through legal procedure but through logistics. The IOM’s voluntary return program, he says without hesitation, is not voluntary. People sign because they have no alternative.

The EU has provided a great deal of money, Kamara says, and the state has been given carte blanche to deploy it as it sees fit. When European delegations visit, things get cleaned up. Detention sites are emptied. Walls receive a fresh coat of paint. The delegation leaves satisfied. The violence and abuse return.

What makes the Mauritanian case particularly sharp is that the consequences extend well beyond migrants. Kamara himself, a Black man, now carries his identity documents wherever he goes. Without them, he could be stopped and deported, regardless of citizenship, regardless of birthright. The enforcement apparatus, calibrated to identify Black bodies as presumptively foreign, cannot reliably distinguish between a Malian migrant and a Mauritanian national.

When we arrived in Nouadhibou, we spent several days trying to speak to migrants. The neighborhoods where migrant communities would rent small rooms were largely empty. Police had swept through them. People were hiding and afraid to talk.

Nouadhibou used to be, as Kamara describes it, a melting pot — Senegalese, Malian, Gambian, Guinean workers drawn by the fishing economy and a port that needed labor. That city still exists in memory. What has changed is the fear. Communities that once moved openly have learned to disappear.

What is also driving people out is the Atlantic itself. In 2024, according to the NGO Caminando Fronteras, nearly 10,000 people died or went missing attempting the crossing to the Canary Islands — making it the deadliest migration route in the world. Of those, around 6,800 had departed from Mauritania. Traditional fishing pirogues, built for coastal waters, carry up to 200 people into conditions they were never designed for. The distance from Mauritania to the farthest Canary Island is close to 1,000 miles of open Atlantic.

In the offices of the Mauritanian coastguard, the senior officer and captain who receives us sits behind stacks of paper and pulls out his phone. He shows us footage from July 2025: a large pirogue from Guinea-Bissau. Dead bodies on a beach. A man badly beaten — violence erupts in the narrow space between 200 people on open water. Then he pauses on one image. A woman lying dead on the pier. Beside her, still alive, a child of two or three years old.

“It is a tragedy! Even trained military, physically strong men — this will haunt you for life,” he says, crossing his arms. “Maybe not now, but later.” He is grateful we came. When people from outside witness this, he reflects, it reminds him that what he and his staff endure every day is not normal and should never become normal. “It is not normal.”
It has nonetheless become routine.
In Brussels, that routine looks like success.

The EU’s migration partnerships follow a consistent logic: money and concessions in exchange for control. Each agreement is framed in the language of partnership and shared interest. Each produces a metric — fewer crossings — that European governments can present as proof of effectiveness.

What the metric does not capture is displacement. When routes close, people do not stop moving. They find longer, more dangerous paths. The sharp rise in Atlantic crossings over recent years is itself partly a consequence of tightening in the central Mediterranean and on the Libya-Tunisia route. The geography of death shifts; the death toll does not fall.

Nor does the metric capture what happens to those who are stopped. The people Kamara assists — detained in converted schools, deported without legal process, stripped of their belongings in overnight raids — do not appear in the statistics as a cost. They appear, if at all, as a success.

In a hotel resort bathroom, we met Binta, from Freetown, Sierra Leone, working as a cleaner at a hotel in Nouakchott for roughly two to three US dollars a day, sending what she can to her children and father back home. She has been in Mauritania for two years, but wants to leave. Over the week, we tried to reconnect but couldn’t get in touch. Upon leaving the field, a voice message arrived. She had been detained by the police. The crackdown had swept through, and the silence we had registered as simply a gap turned out to have been an arrest.

To understand what is happening on Mauritania’s coast, it is necessary to look east, toward a Sahel the EU’s border partnerships tend to treat as a source of pressure to be managed rather than a crisis to be understood.

In Nouakchott, in his office, just next to the remains of the G5 Sahel headquarters, we meet Cheikh, the government coordinator responsible for development and refugee response in Hodh Ech Chargui, Mauritania’s eastern region, which shares 1,200km of largely unmarked frontier with Mali. The numbers he gives us are striking. Mberra refugee camp was established in 2012 for 60,000 to 70,000 people. It now holds somewhere between 258,000 and 300,000 — with new arrivals every day. More than 40% of the region’s entire population is now made up of people who fled Mali. Mberra, he says quietly, is becoming the second largest city in Mauritania after Nouakchott.

The people arriving are fleeing a conflict that has fractured beyond simple description: jihadist armed groups, separatist factions, and a government whose operations are now conducted alongside Russia’s Africa Corps. Each targets communities perceived as aligned with the others. Civilians flee in all directions, across a border that exists on paper but not on the ground, toward family members on the other side who absorb them without registration.

This is the regional context the EU’s Mauritania partnership largely ignores. The pressure building on Mauritania’s Atlantic coast is inseparable from the collapse of state authority in Mali, the proliferation of armed actors across the Sahel, and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of people with nowhere stable to go. Treating Mauritania as a buffer, paying it to hold the line, addresses none of this. It adds another layer of coercion onto people already moving between armed groups, state violence, and open water.

Cheikh himself makes the development argument clearly: you cannot stop migration at Nouadhibou. By the time someone reaches the coast, the decision has already been made. Investment must go upstream — into border communities, agriculture, livelihoods, education. He makes this case to EU delegations regularly.

Not everything we encountered pointed in the same direction. At the yellow building housing Nouadhibou’s municipality, a well-kept garden out front, sunflowers, red roses, and palm trees, the deputy mayor receives us. She is a politician who takes visible pride in what her office provides. We visit the municipal school, where Senegalese, Malian, Cape Verdean, and Mauritanian children learn together. “We tell the children they are all number one,” she says. The municipality receives no EU funding. Its logic of service provision, at least here, includes everyone.

It is a small thing, and it does not undo what is happening in the streets and at the border. But it is a reminder that the hostility generated by the EU’s partnerships is not the only possible response to the same reality. Other choices are being made, by other actors, in the same city.

The cemetery representative — in his black suit, white shirt, and sunglasses — who walked with us through the sandy graves is also a municipal employee. He documented the dead, prayed for them, requested more space for them, and was present when the body arrived on the orange stretcher. He did not look away.

figure.figcaption: Unmarked graves at the edge of Nouadhibou’s cemetery, where migrants who drowned crossing the Atlantic are buried. Photo by Ahlam Chemlali, March 2026.

div.p: Back at the hotel lobby, France 24 runs on a loop in the background. Analysts are being asked about the people fleeing the latest US and Israeli strikes in Lebanon and Iran. The coastguard officer told us the boats now carry Syrians, Afghans, and Bangladeshis — people who have crossed the Sahara to reach the Mauritanian coast and attempt the Atlantic. As long as wars continue and states collapse, these routes will draw people whom no partnership agreement will deter, because what they are fleeing is worse than the crossing.

The EU presents itself, especially in the current moment of global fracture, as a defender of a rules-based international order, a normative power committed to human dignity and the protection of the vulnerable. These are not empty words. They reflect a genuine tradition, one that matters more, not less, as that order erodes elsewhere.

But they cannot coexist with a policy that pays authoritarian governments to detain people in detention centers, deport citizens by mistake, and leave the unidentified dead in unmarked graves at the edges of cemeteries that are running out of room. The falling numbers that European governments cite as success are not a measure of solution. They are a measure of how effectively the violence and death have been moved out of sight.

The question the EU has not answered, and has largely avoided asking, is what kind of international actor it intends to be. A bloc that exports its values, or one that outsources its borders. A partner to the vulnerable, or a financier of the states that contain them.
In Nouadhibou, the answer is already being written. In wet cement, in letters that barely hold their shape, at the edge of a cemetery only expanding.

entry.summary: European officials are calling the EU-Mauritania migration deal a success. Here’s what the numbers don’t count.

entry.title: Why the US should not recognize Somaliland

div.p: Steven A. Cook argues in a recent piece on “Why the United States Should Recognize Somaliland” that the main reason for recognizing Somaliland is geostrategic. The stakes at play are “confronting the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] and the Houthis as well as shoring up freedom of navigation” (through the Strait of Hormuz and, by extension, the Red Sea and the Suez Canal). He mentions in his account that besides many positive aspects, there were some problems in Somaliland. Concretely, he stresses that “there is opposition to the government among some clans, especially in the east, where sentiment runs in favor of ties with Mogadishu rather than Hargeisa — Somaliland’s capital. This raises the possibility of violent inter-clan conflict in Somaliland. It is a legitimate concern. The good news is that [Somaliland’s President] Irro says he is committed to peaceful dialogue.” This is quite naïve, or willingly ignores the more complex facts. The opposition of those clans in the east is long-standing. Somaliland actually never really controlled the eastern territories, except Lasanod from 2007 to 2022. Armed rebellion emerged there as early as 2009, and in 2023 the militias of the clans in the east defeated the Somaliland army. Since then, a new administration, the North East State (NES) of Somalia, has been established there. Its capital is Lasanod. The NES is recognized by the government in Mogadishu. In August 2026, the Somali prime minister visited Lasanod to discuss, among other things, establishing a base of the Somali National Army (SNA) there. This means that external pushes for Somaliland’s legal independence will likely trigger not only inter-clan conflict but war. In any case, this is well beyond “peaceful dialogue,” and President Irro’s legitimacy ends, at the latest, in Oog, which is an Isaaq-inhabited town some 85 kilometers west of Lasanod. Isaaq, as a rule, support Somaliland. Members of the Dhulbahante and Warsangeli clans in the east typically are Somali unionists.

Steven A. Cook continues in his text that “even taking into account this problem [the contestation of Somaliland in the east], Somaliland stands in contrast to Somalia itself, which has been a fount of terrorism, piracy, and extremism in the Horn of Africa for decades.” Now, ask yourself why Somalia is in such bad shape. Just recall the interventions conducted or backed by the US in Somalia, starting with “Restore Hope” in 1992, which was aborted in 1994, and continuing with the counterterrorism interventions conducted by Ethiopia in December 2006, strongly supported by the US. The first intervention actually fueled the market of violence in Somalia. Some warlords were elevated to “partners” (potential presidential candidates), others were considered villains. When US troops attempted to arrest Mohamed Farah Aideed, they were attacked in the streets of Mogadishu. “Black Hawk Down” ended in 18 Marines being killed and partly mutilated and foreclosed direct US engagement abroad for years. Thus, Washington resorted to indirect interventions, financing warlords and encouraging Ethiopia to do the dirty work in Somalia, especially when, after 9/11, Somalia was (partly wrongly, as declassified US secret service sources show) considered a hotbed of Islamic terrorism. Washington sanctioned the extremely brutal Ethiopian intervention from December 2006 onward, in which thousands — many of them civilians — were killed in Mogadishu and the surrounding areas. This carnage was a main reason why Somalis from across the Horn, including Somaliland, started viewing al-Shabaab as a legitimate defender of the Somali nation. Until the end of 2006, al-Shabaab had a few hundred active fighters. By mid-2007, this number had grown to several thousand, with some young men coming from Hargeysa and elsewhere in Somaliland to volunteer to defend Mogadishu against the Ethiopians (and the Ugandans and Burundians who had entered after February 2007 as part of the African Union mission, which also caused havoc for years). Counterterrorism produced massive terrorism in Somalia and made al-Shabaab big (see here for a longer argument).

Now, just briefly: Compare what came out of the many interventions in Somalia with what came out of non-intervention in Rwanda. When the genocide happened in Rwanda in mid-1994, the UN and the US actively ignored it, refusing to openly state what many already knew — that genocide was happening, and that one could have seen it coming. This was extremely tragic and cost the lives of at least 800,000 people, if not more. But ex-post, one could say that non-intervention allowed the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), Paul Kagame’s army, to end the genocide and establish a new and stable Rwanda. And yes, the RPF itself likely killed hundreds of thousands of fleeing Hutu; and yes, Rwanda turned into an authoritarian state, and human rights are precarious, especially for opposition members. But the same could be said about Uganda, Ethiopia, and, in part, even Israel. The latter are reliable friends of Washington, it seems. So let’s be honest: Human rights do not count when it comes to political interest.

The lesson to be drawn is this: Interventions in Somalia perpetuated conflict and instability. The, back then tragic, rejection to intervene in Rwanda in retrospect proved a factor supporting the building of a stable country after brutal conflict. To argue, as Steven A. Cook does, that Somalia is “a fount of terrorism, piracy, and extremism” is dishonest; it is, as Roland Marchal has argued a while ago, also distorting critical analysis; finally it is a sign of a quasi-colonial argument being made here. Somalis are presented as “unable” to keep political order. Yet, many of Somalia’s problems since 1991 (and even in the 1980s, during the Cold War) have been co-produced by the US and its allies in the Horn of Africa.

Now, to come back to Somaliland: Any intervention to recognize Somaliland against the will of Somalia and many Somalis in the region (including the clans in the east of Somaliland, which today is the North East State of Somalia) is likely a further contribution to externally created instability. It potentially creates another war in the Somali Peninsula.

entry.summary: Washington’s own record of intervention in the Horn of Africa — not Mogadishu’s — is the strongest case against recognizing Somaliland now.

entry.title: This book was born in the streets

div.p: Often, history is written as a recollection of the past. It is treated as the entry of passive data, only to be archived for posterity. But what happens when history, or its making, runs parallel to its archival process?

This is the opportunity offered by the 2024–2025 youth uprisings in Kenya. They gave us room to make history, to analyze events as they unfolded daily, and to document them at the same time. However, proper analysis and recourse were insufficient to help tilt the scale from the state to the masses.

Nevertheless, the documentation of the contestations between the masses and the machinery of the state has been extensive. They have been documented in music, memes, spoken word, poems, graffiti, murals, and essays such as our recent scrapbook titled From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go.

As a contribution to the struggle, From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go collects essays from an intergenerational tapestry of activists, community organizers, writers, and legal minds. It is a conversation between the old and the new, produced in the trenches of the youth uprisings, forging an intergenerational continuum of resistance.

The question of sovereignty appears in all the discussions in From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go. From the streets to the book, external interference in the country’s affairs has been a constant reminder of the incomplete independence we gained in 1963.

One of the book’s main sovereignty concerns stems from the role of multilateral lending institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Some contributors have also analyzed this very question by focusing on the rising foreign military “partnerships” with countries such as the UK, which runs the oldest foreign military unit in Kenya, the British Army Training Unit Kenya (BATUK), which was set up at independence in 1964. Similarly, the US operates Camp Simba and Manda Bay Airfield, and Emmanuel Macron is the new entrant in these defense “cooperations”; his government signed a defense and security partnership with the Kenyan government, which saw 800 French troops visit Mombasa in May 2026 for an exercise under the agreement.

The book also looks at ongoing cooperation between different Kenyan police units with the Israeli state, which is known for gross violations of human rights. Israel continues to equip the Kenyan police with further skills and technology to enable extensive monitoring of protestors, activists, community organizers, and journalists who are considered dissidents.

We also discuss the Seed and Plant Varieties Act of 2022, which sought to criminalize the saving, sharing, and exchanging of uncertified seeds. For many across the country, this was seen as a takeover of our food system. Labeling indigenous seeds and cultivars as uncertified would have made way for agricultural corporations to create a monopoly on the seed market, giving them a firm grip on our food system. Thankfully, through organizing, the act was defeated in November 2025, when the High Court of Kenya in Machakos declared sections of the act unconstitutional.

From the publishing of the book to the launch, we have had our fair share of challenges. The process has been full of fear, tension, and intimidation, but also one full of courage and determination. After months compiling our voices through the essays, proofreading and editing, the manuscript was ready for publishing. Kenya, being a nation with a considerable size of progressive forces and some level of political freedom, we never anticipated that the book would be “too hot a potato to handle” for most publishing houses. The title scared every potential publisher in the country, comrades, and even some safe spaces that we initially thought could provide a home for the book.

We got many suggestions from different quarters to revise the manuscript title to From Mau Mau to Gen Zs. Various justifications were given for why it was a bad idea to proceed with the current title. Some saw it as a way of exposing ourselves too much, while others felt the state might misinterpret the title. As a contributor and one of the people who were involved in its various processes, I knew that the title came with its fair share of risks and burdens to shoulder, but we were all ready for it. To us, “Ruto Must Go” was not just a slogan or a fleeting chant, but a movement that understood what Ruto or Rutoism represented. “Ruto Must Go” meant death to the system whose image is mirrored in Ruto’s presidency. It means uprooting the more than 60-year foundation of the colonial-neocolonial state that Kenya has been; abolishing state capture, misgovernance, deep-rooted corruption, greed, and neocolonial servitude. In the book, Ruto is an epitome of what African youth are loudly rejecting. And for these reasons, we chose to remain with our bold and daring title.

In Kenya, we failed to secure a publisher, and no one seemed interested in supporting us in any way. Luckily, from the most unlikely corner of the growing and ferocious East African “dictatorship states,” we found an oasis of intellectual refuge and solidarity in Uganda, through the Editors’ House Facility. After the publication of the book, 300 copies were printed, and the first 200 copies were dispatched to Kenya at the end of May 2026. Our launch, which was to coincide with the June 1 Madaraka Day celebration (the declaration of internal self-governance), failed to take place as we learned that the books were confiscated at the Kenya-Uganda border. To date, the authorities have failed to release these books.

The driver of the bus that was ferrying the books contacted us and described how he was interrogated and told that they were illegal material in Kenya. He was full of anxiety after being interrogated aggressively for a long period at the border. Through other covert means, we managed to get 55 copies through the border and, later, 45 copies. After we got the copies, we hoped to get the help of some progressive libraries and spaces to help with stocking and distribution, but they distanced themselves.

Luckily, we managed to get Mathare Social Justice Centre (MSJC) as our first stockist and anchor partner in planning for resource mobilization for the first launch. Also, Nuria Bookstores and Cheche Bookshop agreed to stock and distribute the book despite the growing intimidation.

In Mathare, the host of the launch venue was called multiple times by officers at a local police station, informing him to stop the launch after the poster was shared widely. He was summoned to the police station on the eve of the first launch. On the same day, several armed police officers stormed the MSJC offices. Even though they never arrested anyone or asked for the book, they interrogated staff and looked around the bookshelves. Despite this, members of the community came out in greater numbers than we had anticipated.

To avoid disruption on the launch day, the main gate leading to the hall was closed to deny entry to civilian-clothed police officers who kept an eye on the area the whole day. Community members even used a hidden entrance, outsmarting the police who awaited them at the main gate.

The Cheche launch, which targeted activists and writers, went well without any challenges. For the main launch, we were denied several venues, but we managed to get the August 7 Bomblast Memorial Park, which was built to remember the August 7, 1998, US Embassy in Nairobi bombing. With the booking of this venue, the details of the event were not revealed, as that would have caused another cancellation. This event also went well despite the presence of plainclothes officers who hung around the venue and, at one time, came to the park wanting to gather information about the book launch. The media that were invited failed to come to give the event coverage, and the few that came failed to air the launch. As a result, we turned to activists and community journalists, using social media pages and their circles, to spread the “new gospel” in town.

Following the book launch, plans began for the second anniversary of the June 2024 uprisings. From the beginning, this was envisioned as a commemoration and not a protest like the 2025 anniversary. Letters of notification were served to different police stations, including the infamous Central Police Station, where Albert Ojwang lost his life under very suspicious circumstances. On this day, we had planned to lay flower wreaths at Parliament, at spots where protestors were killed, and near important monuments such as the Dedan Kimathi statue. A week before, the government led by President Ruto and his loyal lieutenants were beating the drums of war and promising to “deal” firmly with protestors. Some of his closest allies, including those holding critical security dockets, issued intimidating statements, warning those who planned to participate in the commemorations.

We woke up to a barricaded city, despite the government’s chest-thumping assurances that June 25 would be a normal working day. All roads leading to the city were barricaded, with heavily armed police erecting roadblocks every two to three kilometers. Commuters were left to walk several kilometers to access the city, while being harshly interrogated as if they were treasonous people. In long queues, Kenyans were frisked while getting to the central business district, just like in the colonial days when Africans, armed with their kipande (passcard), were subjected to racial laws that made their access to the city highly controlled and troublesome.
Without a doubt, on June 25 it was illegal to have a Kenyan flag, flowers, or candles — they made you a target.
It was a crime to be a patriotic citizen.

The few who made it to the city, like me, spent most of the time escaping the police surveillance dragnet, formed by a heavy contingent of plainclothes police and uniformed units in balaclavas. Most of the hundreds of us who were arrested while laying flowers in the CBD were charged with the very flimsy offense of obstructing traffic, yet there was basically zero traffic in the city. The police who obstructed traffic on all roads for both motorists and pedestrians decided, ironically, to charge us with the offense that they themselves committed.
Most of us were held for more than 24 hours and denied access to telephones to inform our relatives and friends of our whereabouts.

For those who were abducted, their ordeal was more than horrifying; they were never booked at any police station and endured torture for days, asked repeatedly who was funding them, before being dumped in different locations in Nairobi. Davis Lichuma, a community organizer and activist from Mathare, was abducted on the same day and only released on June 28. He was found heavily tortured and severely traumatized from his ordeal.

With access to the book still limited, we are planning a series of engagements in the coming months to broaden its reach. This will be through the use of the Social Justice Centre’s Traveling Theatre, which will develop scripts and skits for performance in different communities. We will also hold forums in universities to make sure the institutions of higher learning, which were once the voice of reason and organizing, get the inspiration needed to play this role again. Also, we shall have public reading sessions in different parts of Nairobi, especially around areas where people gather in the central business district.
This we will do, as we move from Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go. This book was born in the streets, and to the streets shall it return.

entry.summary: Kenya’s youth uprising was documented in real time through music, murals, memes, and essays. Publishing that history became an act of resistance in its own right.

entry.title: Who killed the Shoga?

div.p: The shoga of the East African coast, a man accepted as a member of women’s society, did not emerge from a vacuum nor from the imposition of outside influence. She was born from the long encounter between Bantu-speaking Africans and Muslim traders from the Arabian Peninsula.

Unlike medieval Christianity, which not only condemned “Sodomites” but sought to prosecute and exterminate them, the posture of classical Islam was categorically different. Liwat [anal intercourse between men] was prohibited, but in practice Islamic jurisprudence was less interested in policing private lives than its Christian counterpart. That was left to Allah’s judgment. Sin may have required repentance, but not necessarily prosecution.

This created a de facto tolerance for discrete same-sex relationships throughout the Muslim world. And not always that discrete. The beloved youth — the ghulam or amrad — appears throughout classical Arabic and Persian poetry, not as a scandalous figure but as a positively conventional object of male desire.

It is into this Islamic cultural framework, transplanted to the East African coast over centuries of trade, settlement, and intermarriage, that the figure of the shoga first appears. The Swahili world was one in which Islam was constitutive — shaping law, poetry, architecture, commerce, and domestic life. Kiswahili reflects this: some 30 percent of its vocabulary derives directly from Arabic. To understand the shoga is to understand how an Islamic cultural tolerance for gender difference was absorbed, transformed, and ultimately owned by the African women who gave the role its name.

Kiswahili-speaking women used the term shoga [pl. mashoga], roughly equivalent to “girlfriend,” as a term of endearment. At some point this term was applied to Swahili men who dressed as women, performed women’s tasks, and were accepted into women’s society. It wasn’t the men who named and defined the shoga. It was the women. This makes any presumed Western equivalent inadequate or misleading.

Furthermore, mashoga were recognized for the social roles they played and were not defined by same-sex desire, either coming from or directed toward them. How did the shoga develop? How did she find her place in society? Written non-Western sources are silent on the subject. Early Arabic travelers and geographers wrote about commerce, politics, and religious practice, not about the interior arrangements of women’s domestic spaces. The shoga was part of the women’s world — sometimes with special ritual or societal functions — smoothly and unproblematically integrated into the whole. What was there to say?

Plenty, once the Europeans started meddling in Swahili affairs. The judgments and pejorative terms followed in a predictable train. Johann Krapf, a German missionary working outside of Mombasa, compiled the first comprehensive Swahili dictionary, in which the secondary meanings of shoga are defined as 1) a “catamite” [a boy kept for sexual purposes by an older man] or passive homosexual partner, and 2) an “impotent” or feminized male.
We see again the Western insistence on defining variant male gender identity not through integrated social roles but through sexual acts. When you only have a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

The hammer in this case was Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, drafted by Thomas Babington Macaulay in 1860 for the British colonial administration. This punished “carnal intercourse against the order of nature” with up to life imprisonment. British administrators exported this provision to their African colonies without qualm — more than half of the world’s remaining sodomy laws are relics of British colonial rule, spanning 17 African countries.

Colonialism didn’t bring same-sex desire and gender variance to sub-Saharan Africa — the historical and anthropological evidence is irrefutable on that point — but it did introduce homophobia. Criminalized now, mashoga had to go underground or into hiding. They were never in control of their own narrative, and generations of missionaries, anthropologists, administrators, and “observers” forced upon them whatever Western sexual-deviant theory was in vogue at the time.

And just when it seemed the mashoga could be permanently dismissed, they were resuscitated and transformed beyond recognition by theories of essentialism imported from the gay liberation movements of the West. They were “born this way” and needed to band together to reclaim their humanity. Shoga was now translated into English as “gay” or replaced by a new word, gei [pl. magei], that LGBTQ Swahilis used to describe themselves with something approaching pride.

Heterosexual Africans who had coexisted with the shoga hated this new identity. The Pride marches, the public declarations, the demands for recognition and legal equality — that was what “homosexuality” came to mean for them. What they were rejecting was not African same-sex practice or gender variance. What they were rejecting was a Western political identity organized around a Western sexual ontology. Of course, the homophobia of the American fundamentalist Christians who flooded into Africa after their domestic defeats on gay rights was equally alien. The culture wars of America are now torching the social fabric of Africa.

And where is the shoga in all of this? Gone. Long gone. Traces of her historical presence exist, as referenced in traditional Swahili epistemology, in oral history, in the memory of the dying generations who were ignorant of Western frameworks of gender variance. But the flesh-and-blood shoga was destroyed twice: first by colonial law and the missionary exegesis that preceded it, then by liberation movements that replaced colonial stigma with Western-style pride. She was never allowed to speak for herself, and we’ll never know what she had to say.

entry.summary: Long before modern sexual identities reached the East African coast, the Swahili shoga occupied a recognized place in women’s society, until colonialism and later Western frameworks remade them.

entry.title: Somalia’s uncertain hand-off

div.p: This week, the Federal Government of Somalia held a domestic security conference in Mogadishu, attended by senior government officials and representatives of the international community. The conference came at a particularly critical time, as Somalia faces a growing dilemma on multiple fronts — the gradual drawdown of the AU mission in the country, the expected closure of international support structures, and an increasing political deadlock between the federal government and some federal member states.

These issues have been compounded by another concern that has grown over the past several months — the continuing threat posed by al-Shabaab and questions over whether the Somali National Army has the capacity to fill the security vacuum that could emerge as African troops are reduced. However, the federal government is projecting far greater confidence in Somalia’s ability to manage the transition than many of its international partners anticipated.

Speaking at the conference, National Security Adviser to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Aweys Haji Yusuf, who is also regarded as an influential presidential ally, said the withdrawal of international missions from Somalia was “the result of a long-term process” rather than a sudden decision. He noted that discussions and “assessments of Somalia’s ability to take greater control” of its own affairs had been underway for more than four years. According to Aweys, the government sought to determine when Somalia would be able to reduce its dependence on the UN, with assessments concluding that Somali institutions were increasingly capable of managing political and governance responsibilities that had previously received substantial UN support.

Somalia’s Minister of Religious Affairs and Endowments, Mukhtar Robow, who previously served as a senior figure in the militant group al-Shabaab before defecting, also addressed the gathering. Robow said Somalia’s security environment had “changed significantly,” adding that the country was now in a stronger position than it was in previous years.

The comments come amid increasingly assertive statements from President Hassan Sheikh’s administration that Somalia is preparing to assume greater responsibility for its own security and governance. Speaking at the Hananbure military training centre in Galgaduud during the graduation of thousands of new Somali National Army recruits, President Hassan Sheikh said international partners had played an important role in supporting Somalia’s fight against a prolonged insurgency, but stressed that reliance on foreign forces could not continue indefinitely.

Somalia is entering one of the most consequential reductions in international support since outside powers began rebuilding the country’s security and political institutions more than two decades ago. Two processes are now unfolding simultaneously. The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS), the political mission that succeeded UNSOM, is due to cease operations on October 31, 2026, completing a two-year transition requested by the Somali government in the name of greater national ownership.
