Its responsibilities — including support for constitutional reform, elections, human rights, the rule of law, security-sector development, and the coordination of international assistance — are being transferred to Somali institutions, the UN Country Team, and other partners.

Separate from that process, however, is an increasingly acute crisis surrounding the nearly 12,000 African troops deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). Those forces depend heavily on the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) for much of the infrastructure that allows them to operate, including food, water, fuel, aviation, medical evacuation, communications, equipment support, and troop transportation. The convergence of the UN political mission’s closure with growing uncertainty over the future of this logistical system means Somalia could lose layers of international political and security support within months of each other, even as al-Shabaab retains a substantial presence across southern and central parts of the country.

The most serious shock has come from Washington. On July 1, Reuters reported, citing a US diplomatic note, that the Trump administration had informed the AU that it would no longer support UNSOS beyond the end of 2026 and would oppose a Security Council mandate continuing UN logistical or operational backing for AUSSOM. UNSOS has an annual budget of roughly $500 million, and diplomats told Reuters that the African mission would be extremely difficult to sustain unless another mechanism replaced it. Washington said it had already provided nearly $2 billion in assessed contributions to UNSOS and its predecessor, and argued that Somalia had failed to assume sufficient responsibility for its security despite years of international assistance.

The decision also followed Washington’s earlier opposition to applying the UN Resolution 2719 financing framework to AUSSOM, which could have placed as much as 75% of eligible mission costs on predictable UN assessed contributions. The shift should not, however, be interpreted as a complete American retreat from counter-terrorism in Somalia. US Africa Command has continued an intensive campaign of air strikes in the country. Rather, Washington appears increasingly prepared to conduct narrowly defined counter-terrorism operations while withdrawing from the expensive multilateral architecture that sustains African peacekeepers and supports Somalia’s longer-term security transition. In a recent interview with local media, AFRICOM commander General Dagvin Anderson expressed frustration over the limited progress made so far.

That decision has triggered a scramble among African troop-contributing countries and the AU to determine whether the mission can be sustained through greater African financing, but the figures illustrate the limits of that approach. Uganda convened Burundi, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Egypt, Kenya, Somalia, and other partners for an extraordinary AUSSOM summit in Kampala, as questions mounted over the mission’s future. Uganda’s military leadership said UNSOS support had already been reduced by about 25% and warned that troop contributors would have to find political and financial alternatives.

The AU has increasingly urged member states to expand contributions to its Peace Fund, implement the long-planned 0.2% levy on eligible imports, and rely more heavily on domestic African resources. However, the scale of the problem was already evident in 2025. AUSSOM required about $196 million for the year, but by late September only $24.6 million had been pledged, including $20 million from the AU, while troop-contributing countries had kept personnel deployed for around 15 months without allowances, effectively subsidizing the mission themselves.

Europe, traditionally the financial backbone of successive AU missions in Somalia, has also become increasingly reluctant to carry the burden indefinitely. The European Union and its member states have provided almost €2.8 billion to AU-led missions in Somalia over roughly two decades, but European governments have been pressing for a gradual reduction in the international security footprint as costs have mounted and questions have persisted over when Somali forces will be capable of replacing foreign troops.

In April 2026, after roughly two years of negotiations over renewed financing, the EU finally approved €75 million for AUSSOM, making Europe the mission’s largest direct financial supporter and providing badly needed money for troop reimbursements and associated support. The contribution is substantial, but it does not resolve the underlying financing problem. The EU grant is far smaller than the broader logistical system operated by UNSOS, and European governments have shown little appetite for simply replacing Washington as the mission’s principal financier. The result has been a continuing search for burden-sharing involving the AU, EU, Britain, and other donors, but without the predictable multi-year financing arrangement African governments have sought.

The strain on AUSSOM is part of a much wider international retrenchment from Somalia. The dismantling of USAID and US foreign-aid cuts have hit programs supporting health, education, economic development, and government capacity. Funding available to aid organizations fell from about $2.2 billion in 2022 to roughly $300 million in 2026, while funding for the acute-malnutrition response fell by more than 80 percent and hundreds of health and nutrition facilities closed or faced closure. At the same time, the dedicated UN political mission that advised Somalia on federalism, elections, justice, security-sector reform, and institution-building is disappearing, leaving more of those responsibilities to a smaller UN country presence and Somali institutions themselves.

The emerging international model is consequently much leaner. Targeted military action against immediate terrorist threats may continue, as the continuing US air campaign demonstrates, but the expensive architecture of peacekeeping, stabilization, humanitarian assistance, and long-term state-building is contracting. For Mogadishu, this has created a mismatch — international partners are increasingly demanding Somali ownership and self-reliance at precisely the moment when the external financing, logistics, and institutional support that helped the state reach its current level of capacity are being scaled back.

The recent and increasingly assertive remarks from federal government officials are intended to demonstrate that Somali authorities are prepared to assume greater responsibility for both the country’s security and political affairs as international involvement declines. The message from Mogadishu is one of growing confidence. Yet the situation on the ground remains far less certain. Somalia continues to face a contested political environment, the absence of a broadly agreed and inclusive electoral framework, and a constitutional crisis that together have complicated efforts to build consensus around the country’s political transition. These disputes do not necessarily negate the federal government’s claim that Somali institutions have become more capable, but they underline the gap between assuming responsibility and achieving the political cohesion required to exercise it effectively.

The security picture is similarly mixed. The government has made important gains in strengthening security in Mogadishu and has expanded and trained elements of the Somali National Army, but al-Shabaab continues to pose a serious threat across large parts of southern and central Somalia and retains the ability to conduct attacks, pressure local communities, and exploit weaknesses in state control. We are also seeing increasing reports of a complicated and murky relationship between al-Shabaab and the Houthis in Yemen as the war on Iran intensifies. At the same time, piracy has re-emerged, despite the presence of multinational maritime forces in Somali waters. Against that background, the federal government’s growing confidence indicates a political signal, particularly as international partners scale back their presence, but it has yet to produce sufficiently tangible progress to resolve the wider doubts surrounding Somalia’s transition.

The central question is therefore whether Somali political and security institutions can consolidate and maintain security stability and build a sufficiently inclusive political settlement as the external structures that have supported the country for more than two decades continue to recede.

entry.summary: As the UN and the US pull back from Somalia’s security architecture within months of each other, Mogadishu insists it is ready. The gap between that confidence and the country’s political reality tells a different story.

entry.title: Reading List: Faraaz Mahomed

div.p: My novel, Mother/Land, focuses on a law professor, Salim, a South African in New York, who finds out that he is the product of an affair between his mother — Sawligha — and an apartheid politician. The story engages with the recent past as well as the apartheid years, telling parallel histories about the Fees Must Fall movement in South Africa, Black Lives Matter in the US, forced removals under the Group Areas Act, and the experience of a Muslim immigrant in New York with a gay Afrikaans brother whose life he might save.

Salim has a sunken world-weariness, which is perhaps rooted in his intellectualization and his provenance. There is no shortage of such protagonists wandering the streets of New York, whether in Herzog, Open City, or Netherland. Interestingly, two of these are also immigrant narratives, although the latter might not characterize itself as such. My own experience as a South African of Muslim origin living in New York certainly shaped the story, but I read We Need New Names with great interest, and I found some of the complexities of Salim and his family in it.

The theme of inheritance is one of the most prominent in Mother/Land. Sawligha and Salim’s relationship is central, and this dialogue in the matrilineal relationship (and to some extent the patrilineal too) had me reaching for On Earth We’re Briefly Gorgeous by Ocean Vuong and The Return by Hisham Matar. These are beautifully gifted writers, not only in their prose, but also in the intimacy with which they write. Looking for intimacy, and for the ‘lostness’ that Salim conjures, I often turned to In a Strange Room — a brilliant and relentlessly personal text.

Sawligha’s arc takes place during the days of the removals. Richard Rive’s Buckingham Palace stood out as a reference text about District Six, but I think my own family history in Vrededorp/Fietas/Fordsburg/Pageview (a cluster neighbourhood in Johannesburg) was a good starting point too. To understand the topography and to build a reliable history of what was left of the district, I relied on Sean Field’s Lost Communities, Living Memories and on South African History Online (a great resource!). The story of Sawligha’s affair with an apartheid politician is pure fiction, but I’d decided that Carl Lamprecht, Sawligha’s lover and Salim’s father, would be a contemporary of DF Malan. I did not read up much on him (merely picking up facts from Wikipedia), but there are small details that have helped to tell the history, and indeed portray Carl as a multidimensional character.

To capture the perfect naïve goodness of Salim, and to engineer (as my editor Fourie likes to say) a version of a person who intellectualizes too much and yet finds himself ultimately wanting, I found something quite akin in The Idiot. The tragedy of it and the beauty of it are very much the stuff of my daydreams — and the bittersweetness of Dostoevsky is something I find really captivating, and has actually helped me write the voice of by far the wisest character in the novel — eight-year-old Aa’isha.

I struggled with Aa’isha, Salim’s daughter, who sees the intricacies of the world and endeavors to understand them, all the while feeling like the contradictions and the lies that adults tell themselves are utterly nonsensical. It was a creative growth path for me personally, and I spent an inordinate amount of time reading everything from The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time to The Girl with the Louding Voice to try (and very possibly fail) to get the words, the logic, the temperament, and the reality of Aa’isha right.

As a psychologist, I went back to Piaget and Erikson, but the truth is that I am under no illusions that the voice is marked by a precociousness that I couldn’t quite erase (and that, by the final edit, I had decided was just the right amount of weird, unreliable humanness). I think that’s part of the beauty of writing children, though — because they do turn out to be the most astute of characters, even when their vocabularies don’t quite match their insight.

Reading Zuleika Dobson helped with the metaphysical aspects of my storytelling (Sawligha is, after all, a ghost), but I enjoyed telling the paranormal aspects with a recognition of their ambivalent relationship to reality. Olga Tokarczuk’s House of Day, House of Night is mystifying, and Ben Okri’s Famished Road trilogy contains beautiful stories about the ability to travel between worlds. I am indebted to these, and so many other writers for the gifts of their work.

entry.summary: How do the struggles of one generation echo, decades later, in another’s?

entry.title: Who started Nollywood?

div.p: Here is the short version of a story that has been told wrong for 30 years.

Kenneth Nnebue was born in Mgbidi, Imo State. He left school after sixth grade and apprenticed under his brother, a handbag maker, before entering trade himself in the Onitsha market. By the late 1980s, he was in Lagos, importing VHS tapes from Taiwan, distributing pirated foreign films, and trying to move product in a difficult economy. When the tapes stopped selling, he put an original story on them instead. That story — Living in Bondage (1992) — cost 150,000 naira, about $7,000 at the time. It sold over 100,000 copies in its first weeks through informal markets in Lagos, Enugu, and beyond. It launched a global industry.

What gets left out of most tellings: before Nnebue made Living in Bondage in Igbo, he had already produced at least 27 Yoruba-language films. An Igbo trader, operating in Lagos, making Yoruba content, who then made the Igbo film the world decided was the beginning of everything. The ethnic ownership of that origin — who gets to claim Nollywood, which tradition gets the credit, which city gets the heritage tourism — has been contested ever since. Not because the evidence is unclear, but because resolving it requires someone to say plainly what Nollywood actually is: an art form rooted in Yoruba theatrical tradition, or an industry born from an Igbo trader’s logistics problem. These are different things. The confusion between them is not innocent.

The Yoruba side of the argument is not a retroactive claim. The Yoruba Traveling Theater tradition, Alárìnjó, reaches back to the 19th century. Its modern form is usually traced to Hubert Ogunde, whose touring theater company toured Nigerian cities through the 1950s and 1960s, its work politically sharp enough that a regional premier banned it outright. That stage tradition migrated to celluloid film through the 1970s and 1980s, and by 1985 Moses Olaiya’s Mosebolatan was one of the country’s first genuine blockbusters. Critically, Yoruba filmmakers moved onto VHS format in 1988, four years before Living in Bondage. If the question is who touched the video format first, it wasn’t Nnebue.

So why does his name carry all the credit? Because Living in Bondage wasn’t first, but it was the first to look like it knew what it was doing, packaged with a glossy, full-color cover styled after pirated Hollywood tapes, presented as a professional product instead of a stopgap. The story helped too — a man who joins an occult society and sacrifices his wife for wealth, only to be haunted by what he’s done — landed hard in a country deep in structural adjustment-era desperation, when stories of ritual money were part of the cultural air people breathed. And despite being shot entirely in Igbo with no subtitles for a full year, the film crossed ethnic lines anyway — co-producer Okey Ogunjiofor would later say simply that people who didn’t understand the language still understood the story, because the pictures carried it.

What Nnebue actually contributed, then, wasn’t the invention of video filmmaking — Yoruba practitioners had that four years earlier. He contributed a “template,” an industrial model of direct-to-video production that the entire industry would replicate for the next two decades. Every straight-to-video Nollywood film that followed, regardless of language, was built on the business logic Nnebue stumbled into while solving an unglamorous warehouse problem.

Laid side by side, these two histories aren’t actually contradictory; they’re answering two different questions. It’s the single phrase “who started Nollywood” that collapses them into one, forcing a false contradiction. The Yoruba lineage answers where the art form came from. The Nnebue story answers where the industry came from. Ogunde’s company built the grammar. Nnebue’s warehouse problem built the factory.

I’m writing this from Enugu, one of the cities where Living in Bondage first sold by the hundreds in market stalls. Here, Nollywood’s Igbo roots aren’t distant history but lived memory, passed down the way a family recipe is. That memory is real. So is Ogunde’s banned theater company. Neither one needs to lose for the other to be true.

But Nigeria rarely lets cultural origin stay this generous. Who started Nollywood is never just a historical question here — it’s tied to tourism revenue, festival programming, whose language gets state funding, whose grandchildren get to say “we built this.” Thirty years on, the debate hasn’t been resolved because resolving it was never really the point. Someone benefits from the ambiguity every time it stays open, and someone loses something every time it closes.
That, more than the biography of one trader from Mgbidi, is the story worth telling.

entry.summary: Kenneth Nnebue made 27 Yoruba-language films before Living in Bondage. Why does Nigeria still only remember the one he made in Igbo?

entry.title: On Safari

div.p: Ever since the World Cup concluded with Spain’s emphatic triumph over universally loathed Argentina (at least it felt this way), it has no longer felt like everyone is looking in the same direction at the same time. For a month and a bit, football’s biggest stage gave us one of the last remaining experiences of shared, global time. Not global justice, not global equality — the tournament is in many ways a monument to their absence — but a crude, synchronized schedule. Games at set hours, short-lived solidarities, the impression, however false, that the world is briefly doing something together, undergoing a collective experience.

Once that all ends, you’re plunged back into a social temporality and news cycle that moves at lightning speed and adjusting back is disorienting. It didn’t help that I had to deal with a debilitating case of cyclosporiasis (in an ill-fated decision, I tried some Taco Bell for the first time the day before my return flight back to South Africa, and getting a food-borne illness felt like an appropriate parting gift from a United States in decline). In the weeks since the World Cup, I found myself in a kind of fog I at first attributed to being exhausted from a busy year coupled with bouts of illness, but which, as I return to relatively decent health, I recognize as a familiar feeling, one that has typified contemporary experience for as long as I can remember.

There’s a book by the Polish sociologist Zygmunt Bauman which I think is underrated, and does better at capturing the texture of our epoch than many other attempts (do we live in late capitalism, surveillance capitalism, the burnout society, post-modernity, etc etc.). It’s called Liquid Modernity, and Bauman’s straightforward argument is that the defining feature of contemporary society is no longer the construction of stable institutions, identities, and social relationships, but their constant dissolution. Where the “solid” phase of modernity sought to build enduring structures — stable careers, lifelong marriages, nation-states, political parties, class identities, and fixed moral frameworks — our present condition is “liquid”: forms no longer retain their shape for long enough to organize human life. The contradictory result of this is that even though in many important respects, individuals have unprecedented freedom (at least compared to any other point in human history), it’s coupled with chronic insecurity and the burden of constantly having to remake ourselves.

One of his most evocative concepts is the notion of pointillist time, which is “more prominent for its inconsistency and lack of cohesion than for its elements of continuity and consistency.” Time under liquid modernity is fragmented and disconnected, and rather than unfolding as a series of events with some relationship to each other, it is rather a series of “eternal instants.” It’s not hard work to see how this characterizes so much of algorithm-dominated society in general, and our media consumption in particular. If it wasn’t hard enough figuring out what producing any meaningful “content” takes in the attention economy, it was dismaying for me to recently learn that even new media like podcasts and video essays are themselves now being repurposed in a “clipping economy” where increasingly, circulation of short clips from longer pieces is becoming the main event rather than previews.

At Africa Is a Country, we are very proud of our World Cup Road Trip series. Three episodes are live — Episode 1 on the Cabo Verdean diaspora in New England, Episode 2 on the affinity between Algeria and Lawrence, Kansas, and Episode 3 on Toronto’s Ghanaian community — with further episodes from the road currently in post-production. Although the website and our weekly newsletters remain our bread and butter, like most outlets, we are experimenting with different ways of reaching audiences, and short-form video has been one of them. The newsletter in particular functions as our most reliable direct channel to readers as social platform referrals grow less dependable. The World Cup, however, gave us a powerful on-ramp: sport brought in readers who might not otherwise arrive at a piece on visa regimes or xenophobia, and the coverage was built to convert that interest into political understanding.

What has been challenging is that discovery is now heavily platform-dependent, and the same work travels very differently depending on where it lands: our road trip episodes have found nearly 10,000 views on Instagram while the identical material moves far more slowly on YouTube. And we’re a small team that only ever has the capacity to make something and release it into the world once, maybe twice. How much labor is involved in reproducing countless clips from one piece, and circulating it on an innumerable number of platforms? Whatever it is, we simply cannot do it.

In fact, we are behind on our production and release schedule, and as is normal to do, we worry about whether the material will be stale by the time we are ready to publish it. To be sure, timeliness is always an objective in journalism, and has been before the age of platform dominance. In fact, what we are dealing with now is tougher to pin down. Bauman’s concept of pointilist time captures, on the one hand, the way discrete events move differently under liquid modernity, and how our sense of when things are happening is transformed. But algorithmic time also organizes the field of perception, i.e, our sense of where things are happening, or more precisely, of what is happening. In other words, the hyper-personalization of what we see means it is increasingly difficult to be certain that we are seeing the same thing, and interpreting the same set of events.

Naming what’s happened to our sense of what needs a different word, and the nearest one I can find is the concept of anamorphosis. Hans Holbein’s 1533 double portrait The Ambassadors is the textbook case. Two French diplomats flank a shelf crowded with globes and instruments, and stretched across the floor between their feet is a long grey smear that reads, from where you’re standing to look at the men, as nothing at all — a flaw in the paint, maybe. Walk up close and look from a sharp angle, low down on the right, and the smear resolves into a human skull, rendered in as much detail as anything else in the frame. Both images are actually there on the same canvas. Neither is a distortion of the other. Stand in one place, and you see two wealthy men and their instruments; stand in the other, and the whole painting turns out to be about death, and you cannot hold both pictures in your eye at once. So, the feed isn’t handing everyone a blurred or partial version of one picture. It’s resolving the same underlying material into fully coherent, mutually exclusive pictures, depending on where — which feed, which platform, which slice of the personalization engine — you happen to be standing at.

Although the World Cup directed our attention to one shared happening, what one’s experience of the World Cup largely depended on was whether you were simultaneously experiencing it online, and if so, primarily through which platform, etc. For example, while Argentina’s seemingly unsportsmanlike conduct and perceptions of favoritism made them wildly unpopular online, that didn’t translate for most regular people I spoke to who still associated it with Maradona and the global South and couldn’t believe anyone in Africa could cheer for Spain. Since at least Qatar 2022, the World Cup has increasingly felt asynchronous on this dimension, consisting of several overlapping tournaments, each with its own villains, injuries, scandals, and moral weather.

Now, of course, every attempt to make sense of the world begins from the fact that each of us encounters it from our own irreducibly subjective position. Human experience is always an exercise in interpretation: the attempt to establish shared meaning across common or divergent experience. What feels distinctive about the present moment, however, is that we are losing not simply a shared sense of time, but a shared world. Politics has always depended on more than disagreement. It has depended on the possibility that we are, in some meaningful sense, disagreeing about the same reality — that our arguments begin from a common object, however differently we interpret it. What has become fragile is the achievement of that common world: not identical beliefs, but enough shared ground to know that we are talking about the same events, inhabiting the same present, looking at the same object from different sides. At least in the group stages, the World Cup felt like it briefly restored a condition that democracy, journalism, and ordinary social life all depend on, namely shared attention. But as the competition narrowed and the algorithm regained its grip, the World Cup itself increasingly dissolved into the endless circulation of content, re-entering the attention economy as just another stream of commodities competing for visibility.

Perhaps the World Cup has simply become too big a spectacle, one exceeding our capacity to engage with it meaningfully at the scale it’s now played at, and perhaps the future will warrant a return to “doing things at human scale.” Staying with football: it’s felt, in recent years, like women’s football has become popular partly for this reason. This isn’t to make light of the real disparities in investment and coverage that still shape the women’s game. But there’s a sense in which it still feels within reach — legible at something closer to human scale, not yet fully run through the same algorithmic churn the men’s tournament now is.

Which brings me, with some embarrassment, to WAFCON. Morocco has been hosting the tournament since late July, and we’re already two days away from the semifinals — the tournament’s own answer to the question of scale above. Smaller broadcast footprint, thinner commercial saturation, a fraction of the men’s tournament’s algorithmic weight. It would have been the perfect subject for the argument I’ve just spent several thousand words making.

We have not covered it properly. Contributing editor Maher Mezahi has been filing dispatches on his podcast and newsletter, but the rest of us have been largely silent, and that’s doesn’t reflect anything except an editorial oversight. I don’t want to paper over it with a joke about being like tired footballers at the end of a long season, true as that joke also happens to be (and if only we had as many resources at our disposal). The honest version is that a small team, mid-fog, still finishing a World Cup series that had already outrun its own schedule, let a second tournament pass it by — which is, if I hold myself to my own argument rather than just making it, exactly what this piece has been describing. Not a failure of will, but what happens when the volume of things worth attending to exceeds what we can hold.

So, I end with an apology, and an announcement. We’re going on our bi-annual publishing break this week, later than planned and more tired than usual, in no small part because of everything above. We’ll be back with something on WAFCON’s back end — the final is on the 16th — and whatever else the world has rearranged the calendar around by the time we’re attempted to rest. For now the fog wins this round. We’re stepping out of it on purpose, rather than being carried along by it, which is about the only kind of victory on offer.

entry.summary: This publishing break, we contemplate why we’re all feeling so burnt out.

entry.title: A border spectacle

div.p: What happened last Thursday in Ceuta was a border spectacle of surprising scale and scope. Tens of thousands of mainly young fellow Moroccans stormed the gates while others braved the water to enter the enclave. All the elements of the spectacle were there: from images of boisterous youngsters jockeying for entry, to a diplomatic slanging match, to border patrols scrambling to push migrants back to Morocco.

It sounds like a geopolitical déjà vu — almost the same border antics: scene, actors, protagonists, and victims staged in May 2021. In fact, what happened in Ceuta is the third episode of the border spectacle: the first staged in May 2021, the second in September 2024, and here we are watching the third — and perhaps not the last — episode, marking a shift in Morocco’s migration diplomacy to a more coercive approach.

There is no conspiracy theory behind the Ceuta border spectacle; there is only a geopolitical buildup to understand Morocco’s coercive migration diplomacy. The latter has shifted migration governance from policies, practices, and discourses to the direct use of its youth and other racialized African migrants in diplomatic sparring.

Here is the buildup: On December 10, 2020, the Trump administration recognized Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara. This historic moment led Morocco to garner further diplomatic recognition, especially from its traditional allies — not least Spain as a former colonizer. In January 2021, a diplomatic logjam between Morocco and Germany started to simmer following the latter’s criticism of Donald Trump’s proclamation to recognize Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. This diplomatic friction with Germany prompted Morocco to push the European Union.

Meanwhile, the possibility of meeting Morocco’s expectations, whether by the EU or its member states, proved far-fetched. The diplomatic spat between Morocco and Spain reached its nadir when the latter hosted Brahim Ghali, the leader of the Polisario Front, in April 2021 to seek medical treatment. In a tit-for-tat response, Morocco unleashed over 8,000 migrants, including around 3,000 minors. Santiago Abascal, the leader of the anti-migrant far-right Vox party in Spain, denounced the arrivals, stating Morocco was “launching minors like battering rams” against the Spanish borders.
Now, the same scenario is unfolding after Pedro Sánchez visited Algeria to parley with President Abdelmajid Tebboune over natural gas and Western Sahara.

In Europe, the border spectacle sparked a moral panic that feared the invasion of the southern flanks of Europe, raking up right-wing opprobrium over Sánchez’s progressive yet lax migration policies. Far from being an invasion, the border spectacle staged produced anti-migration fodder for far-right politicians.
The border spectacle has resurfaced the centuries-old colonization of Ceuta and Melilla.

The international public that redeems Sánchez as the proponent of the Palestinian cause and progressive migration reforms is bewildered by Ceuta’s tiny geography at the outer fringe of the African continent, wondering how Spain, and for that matter Europe, will be invaded while in Africa. Some historical context is urgent here to disentangle these “only land borders between Africa and EUrope.”

Depending on one’s geopolitical stance, Ceuta and Melilla are at once enclaves and exclaves. From the colonial standpoint of Spain and the European Union, they are seen as exclaves, embodying the external sovereign extension of Spain and, more recently, Europe. In most academic literature, however, the two cities are enclaves standing as the last remnants of European colonization on the African continent. For Moroccans, the two cities are occupied territories, whose recovery remains an unfinished national project of decolonization.

The dispute over Ceuta and Melilla has shaped a long history of sporadic tensions in the relationship between Morocco and Spain. Its historical roots extend back to the Reconquista (c. 718–1492), culminating in the fall of Al-Andalus, and ended with the expulsion of the Moors, between 718 and 1492, from the Iberian Peninsula to North Africa.

Spain extended its sovereignty beyond the Peninsula to vie for external territorial sovereignty in North Africa, seizing Melilla in 1497 and Ceuta — initially conquered by Portugal in 1415 and then ceded to Spain — in 1668. The two towns served as external bulwarks for the clash between the Ummah of Islam and Christendom. Well into the wake of decolonization, Morocco has never ceased reclaiming the two enclaves, invoking the principle of territorial integrity laid down in the Charter of the United Nations.

In 1991, Morocco and Spain signed a Treaty of Friendship, Good Neighborliness and Cooperation. Yet, in 1995, to complete the political formation of its national sovereignty, Spain granted Ceuta and Melilla the status of Ciudades Autónomas (Autonomous Cities). This move was criticized by Morocco as a breach of the treaty and an insidious attempt to annex the two territories to its national dominion. To parry such criticism, at the end of 1996, Spain formally constructed barriers fencing Ceuta and Melilla, which was justified by Spain — by the appearance of West African migrants as a “new problem” at the external borders of Europe. In September 1997, the then Prime Minister of Morocco, Abdellatif Filali, reiterated this claim at the UN General Assembly, that “Moroccan towns under Spanish occupation” should follow the same resolution pursued by Hong Kong and Macao.

Spain’s accession to the Schengen Treaty in 1995 promptly activated the Europeanization of Ceuta and Melilla. In this sense, the borderwork in the two towns is no longer a national matter but a European one, which requires the joint efforts of the EU, Spain, and Morocco to combat irregular migration. The subsequent fortification of the two towns, the Euro-African frontier, is a prototype of “Fortress Europe” and border externalization. What follows the birth of this fortification of Ceuta and Melilla is a reenactment of colonial violence against racialized migrants.

The border spectacle of Ceuta bears witness to the longue durée of colonial violence and borders as its obdurate, historical residue. It also bespeaks the banality of colonial durabilities over such territorial splinters in the shadow of decolonization. This colonial history has, in turn, shaped how Europe views the mobility of Africans, deploying deficit and imperial frameworks of a ‘crisis,’ ‘problem,’ and ‘threat.’

On October 11, 1995, Policía Nacional repressed a group of black African migrants in Ceuta who were contained and refused relocation to mainland Spain. The event marked a turning point, staging the first ‘border spectacle’ of the Euro-African borders. What followed was unending processes of “bordering and re-bordering” the Moroccan-Spanish borders. In October 2005, exactly ten years later, 15 black African migrants fell dead at the fences around Ceuta and Melilla. Nationwide raids and arrests of migrants in forest camps around the two enclaves were carried out by the Moroccan authorities, dumping over 2,000 black African migrants in the remote desert borderland with Algeria. Almost another decade later, on February 6, 2014, another breaking point of migrant death claimed the lives of another 15 migrants in the Tarajal Massacre. Guardia Civil opened fire on black African migrants as they waded their way into Ceuta along Tarajal Beach. A new lawsuit was later filed against Spain by a Cameroonian survivor. On February 6 of every year, “commemorActions” and sit-ins are held all around the world denouncing migrant death and disappearance.

The most recent breaking point is the Melilla Massacre, which is, in large part, the subject matter and ethnographic groundwork of my thesis. The Melilla Massacre is a historic spectacle of migrant death, claiming the lives of at least 27 black migrants from East Africa. Dozens went missing, others were incarcerated, and survivors were dumped at the Algerian border or dispersed to different urban fringes within Morocco.

Tracing the genealogies of the EU’s border externalization within the longue durée of the colonial matrix allows us to see what happened in Ceuta beyond presentist accounts of migration diplomacy: it allows us to see through the enduring continuum of social death and containment that saps the resourceful subjectivities of Moroccan and African youth at large.

Far less concerned with deciphering the geopolitical palaver of the Ceuta crossings, Moroccan journalists, artists, activists, and intellectuals are resurfacing discussion over the broken social contract between the state and its citizens. The socio-economic malaise plaguing Moroccan youth is a legacy of systemic disinterest in the realities of Moroccans. It favors glamorous investments — as in stadiums for the 2030 World Cup — giving short shrift to basic public services such as health and education. Such legitimate demands were the slogans of the GenZ 212 protests, a grassroots movement born online and driven by young Moroccans, including some of those who stormed the Ceuta border. Many of the protesters were detained, while many chose the ‘backway’ to reach Europe on unseaworthy boats.

From the Moroccan border, the border spectacle of Ceuta is symbolic of an escape from a carceral, postcolonial deathworld — not an invasion or a Moroccan border regime that managed to outfox its Spanish counterpart. Beyond depictions of delinquency, Moroccan youth have proved to be agents of social, economic, and political change, escaping a political juggernaut that grinds down their youth and resourceful subjectivities.

Caminando Fronteras, a Spanish NGO that began counting border fatalities along the Atlantic route in 2015, counted 141 migrant deaths as of August 4. Many more are still missing. Embattled families of mafqudin (missing migrants) are in vertigo, still waiting at the border in hopes of finding their missing relatives. Border Resistance, a collective of migration activists, is monitoring the border violations in Ceuta: the illegal pushbacks, beatings, starvation, and search and identification for the mafqudin among young Moroccans, Sudanese, and Yemeni asylum seekers.

Crossing the borders involves a cultural rite of social death and, upon safe crossing, rebirth. It’s the kind of social death that one escapes from home to seek a new life beyond borders. In the passage, migrants exchange physical death for a new life beyond the Moroccan borders.
For Moroccan migrants, risking their lives along dangerous routes was an escape from the mandibles of social death. The risk promised rebirth and regeneration to individual and communal lives.
Many more Moroccans will continue to reach Ceuta and Europe, undeterred by the unending securitization of borders and the violent deaths and disappearances.

entry.summary: When thousands of young Moroccans stormed Ceuta last week, it was not an invasion, but the latest in a five-year pattern of coercive migration diplomacy on a border with five centuries of colonial history behind it.

entry.title: Between feminism and pan-Africanism

div.p: I read the draft African Charter on Family, Sovereignty and Values the way you read a letter from someone you used to trust. For pages, I was nodding, smiling even. Then I reached my own body on the page, and I understood what the document had done: it had stapled together two tenets of my life that I thought could complement each other, so that to keep one I would have to surrender the other. I always thought my Pan-Africanism gave context and legitimacy to my feminism. This charter disagrees with that.
I am a Pan-Africanist. I am also a feminist. The charter is built so those two cannot share a room.

Let me tell you about the part that got me. When the charter talks about food, it is right. Article 8 asks African states to protect indigenous seeds, to refuse uncontrolled genetically modified seed, to stop criminalizing the farmer-managed seed systems that have fed this continent for millennia, and to put real money — 10 percent of agricultural spending — behind them. When it talks about natural resources, it is right again: removing tariff and non-tariff barriers to intra-African trade to address instability and slow economic growth, no more shipping out raw and buying back finished. Article 9 names the debt trap and our dependence on selling unprocessed commodities. Even its complaint about how treaties get made — the late-night sessions, the documents dumped on delegations in languages and timeframes designed to exhaust them — describes something I have watched happen to African diplomats. On seeds, on minerals, on debt, on the right of Africa to decide for Africa, the charter says things I have spent my life saying.
And then it reaches for my womb, and the same word “sovereignty” turns into a leash.

Article 4 instructs governments to “identify and repeal” any legal instrument that, by its own narrow definition, “undermines the family,” and then names what must go: abortion rights, the legalization of prostitution, the “autonomous sexual rights of minors,” anything it files under “gender ideology,” the “LGBT agenda.” Article 7, while championing the preservation of African health and traditional healing knowledge, reaffirms there is “no international right to abortion” and tells states to reject every reference to sexual and reproductive health in every agreement they touch. Read plainly, that is an instruction to gut the Maputo Protocol, the African Union’s own instrument, which lets a woman end a pregnancy that came from rape or incest, or one that will kill her mentally, financially, or physically. The charter defines marriage as a man and a woman in every legal document, gender as male or female and nothing else. This is not the protection of the African family. It is the government of African bodies.

So here is my problem, and I am not going to pretend it away: I want seed sovereignty, data sovereignty, and the Maputo Protocol. The charter tells me I cannot have all three. I do not accept the premise.

It is worth saying who is holding the staple. A document that accuses sexual and reproductive rights of being a “stealth recolonization” was drafted alongside Family Watch International, an Arizona outfit the Southern Poverty Law Center designates a hate group, whose president trains African legislators to lobby at the UN. It was championed from a State House by a president who has built his late career on the export of anti-gay law. And in its own final article, the charter lists its inspiration: the Geneva Consensus Declaration, the Pompeo/Trump-era American project whose “no international right to abortion” line it copies almost word for word. This is a declaration that Cameroon, my country, along with Uganda, Senegal, Benin, and others, all signed. The thing telling me my health is a colony is itself the import. L’ironie du sort, as francophones would say.

20 governments adopted the charter in Accra; South Africa refused, saying the text could not be reconciled with its Bill of Rights or with the equal marriage rights it grants its citizens, and it was not the only state to abstain. The full list of who endorsed has not been published. The man who hosted and keynoted the conference, who chairs the Conference of Speakers and Presidents of African Legislatures (COSPAL), the continental body now asked to adopt the charter, is the same Speaker who sent Ghana’s own anti-rights bill back for a tidier revote. When a text that claims to speak for the aspirations of African peoples cannot open its own guest list, you have learned something about whose will it is.

I don’t have the solution, and that much honesty is owed. But I know what I will not do, which is let women and queer Africans become the tax we pay for the continent’s dignity. Banning gain-of-function research and toxic pesticides has never required policing a queer African’s body. Owning our minerals has never required a woman to die of a pregnancy we had the law to end. These things should not be in tension. Someone needed them to be, so that I would trade one to win the other.

entry.summary: A charter twenty African governments just endorsed defends seed sovereignty and economic independence in one breath, and moves to gut abortion and queer rights in the next.

entry.title: The prosecutions that never happen

div.p: There is a specific kind of Nigerian newspaper headline I have been reading my whole life. It announces that a former governor, or a minister, or a director-general has been arraigned by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). There are charges. There are counts. The accused person arrives in court in a well-cut agbada, surrounded by lawyers whose fees alone constitute a moderate corruption offence, and they plead not guilty, and the judge grants bail, and the case is adjourned. Then it is adjourned again. Then the administration that appointed the EFCC chairman that filed the charges loses an election, and the new administration appoints a new chairman, and the case against the former governor slows to a pace that makes geological time look urgent.

I am a law graduate. I graduated from the University of Uyo last year. My dissertation was about why this keeps happening, and whether the legal architecture of Nigerian anticorruption enforcement is designed to produce accountability or to produce the performance of accountability. I concluded, after two years of reading statutes and case files and civil society audits, that it is mostly the latter.

The argument is not complicated. Nigeria’s Economic and Financial Crimes Commission was established in 2002 and has operated since then under a chairman appointed by whichever president is in power. That president’s attorney general, a cabinet minister removable by the same president, can take over or discontinue any EFCC prosecution at any stage before judgment, without providing a reason. Five EFCC chairmen have been removed or resigned under circumstances suggesting executive pressure since 2003. The current chairman was appointed by President Bola Tinubu. His predecessor was appointed by President Muhammadu Buhari. The one before that by President Goodluck Jonathan. Each administration has, with minor variation, used the agency to prosecute predecessors and protect allies.

The EFCC announces that it secured over 3,000 convictions between May 2023 and May 2024, a figure confirmed in Freedom House’s 2025 Nigeria country report. This number has been cited internationally, in Freedom House reports and donor assessments, as evidence that Nigeria’s anticorruption effort is producing results. What those 3,000 convictions actually consist of: plea bargains, minor internet fraud cases, and first-instance verdicts that are overturned on appeal. Human Rights Watch found that since the EFCC’s founding, the agency has secured only four convictions against nationally prominent political figures, out of more than 30 arraigned.
Four. Across two decades. In a country where the National Bureau of Statistics has estimated that corruption costs the economy over $18 billion annually.

I want to be honest about what it feels like to grow up inside this. You learn to read the prosecution announcements as political communication rather than law enforcement. When the EFCC arraigns a prominent All Progressives Congress (APC) figure, you note that the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) is probably gaining influence somewhere. When PDP members suddenly accumulate charges, you check the news for who won what election. The Afrobarometer survey from 2023 found that 76 percent of Nigerians believe the EFCC prosecutes based on political instructions rather than evidence. That is not cynicism. That is pattern recognition.

The formal legal problem is straightforward. The EFCC has no constitutional status. It exists by ordinary statute, which means the National Assembly that created it can amend or repeal it, and the executive whose chairman runs it can shape its priorities through appointment. The Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission is constitutionally grounded and requires a two-thirds Senate majority to remove its chairman. The EFCC’s wider mandate, larger budget, and higher public visibility make it the more powerful of the two agencies in practice. But that same power sits on weaker institutional ground, since the president alone controls who runs it and how long they stay. Power without independence is what makes an agency useful as a political instrument, and on that measure the EFCC is the more exposed of the two. Nigeria has, in other words, invested heavily in the institution that is easier to capture and less heavily in the institution that is harder to capture.

There is a reform bill in the House of Representatives that would require the president to nominate the EFCC chairman from a shortlist presented by an independent selection committee. It has been read twice and referred to committee. It will, in all probability, die there. The people who benefit from a capturable EFCC are often the same people sitting on the committees meant to reform it. Several members currently serving on anticorruption oversight committees have themselves been named in EFCC petitions or investigations that never proceeded to trial. A body cannot be expected to legislate away the leverage that protects its own members.

What I keep thinking about, sitting with this, is not the politicians. They are behaving rationally given the incentives. What I think about is the intern at a ministry somewhere who knows where a contract was inflated, who knows which official received the transfer, and who is deciding right now whether to report it. And the thing that should make that decision clear, a legal system that actually prosecutes the corrupt regardless of their political connections, is not available to them. The EFCC’s convictions count includes their cousin’s boyfriend who got arrested for Yahoo-Yahoo. It does not include the person who stole from the hospital where their mother couldn’t get treatment.

The substantive law against corruption is not the problem. Nigeria has had clear statutory prohibitions on financial crimes since 2002. What is the problem is the law that built the EFCC, which handed appointment and removal power over the agency’s leadership to the same office the agency is meant to hold accountable. That is not a flaw in implementation. That is a design choice written into the statute itself, and it guarantees that enforcement bends toward whoever currently controls the presidency.

The prosecution that matters never comes. The case that should terrify the corrupt official managing a stolen contract, that case gets adjourned, or quietly discontinued, or never filed. The 3,000 convictions get announced. And somewhere in Abuja, a very well-dressed man in a very good agbada files a motion for an extension of time, and the lawyers bill their hours, and the judge adjourns to a date not yet fixed, and the money stays where it went.

entry.summary: Nigeria’s anti-corruption agency secures thousands of convictions every year, but when it comes to politically-connected elites, it’s a different story.

entry.title: The price of potential

div.p: At first glance, the cramped quarters of Mafalala, the largest informal settlement in Mozambique’s capital, Maputo, seem to leave barely enough room to play a pass, let alone carve out a football pitch. However, as you weave through the labyrinth of madeira-e-zinco (wood and tin) houses built by workers segregated to the city’s outskirts during the colonial era, you eventually emerge onto a field overseen by a mural of the great Eusébio, the “Phenomenon of Mafalala.” For players like Eusébio to make it to the world’s greatest stage, like in his case, a World Cup final with Portugal in 1966 (Mozambique was a colony of Portugal at the time) or back-to-back European Cups with Benfica in 1961 and 1962, the journey is never a one-man effort.

In Joseph O’Neill’s Godwin, readers are thrown into the shady business of youth African football recruitment. The novel recounts the same types of dealings that propelled players like Eusébio to the game’s pinnacle. The protagonist, Mark Wolfe, a frustrated Pittsburgh-based technical writer, is enmeshed in a resolute mission by his half-brother, Geoff, a desperate British soccer agent, to locate a young West African football prodigy, whom he believes could be the next Lionel Messi.

The narrative follows Mark’s high-stakes quest — which eventually involves a ruthless French talent scout named Lefebvre — and delivers a sharp, darkly comedic critique of modern capitalism and the exploitative, neo-colonial nature of global sports recruitment.

O’Neill deftly illustrates how deeply interwoven football is with the continent’s history and beyond. In a book talk at George Washington University (GWU) that we organized alongside Young Black Professionals in International Affairs (YBPIA), O’Neill dove deeper into the book’s themes. Godwin foregrounds the often-overlooked genesis of African players forging European legacies, the transatlantic nature and exploitative structures of football recruitment in Africa, and the sport’s remarkable capacity to tell human stories worldwide.

For decades, colonial connections, migration, and European recruitment networks have carried African talent across continents. At the 2026 World Cup, 73 players of African birth or descent featured for 12 non-African national teams, yet only around six confirmed African-born players represented European national teams. They are: Marc Guéhi (born in Côte d’Ivoire and representing England, Brice Samba (Republic of Congo and France), Amadou Onana (Senegal and Belgium) Guus Til Samfya (Zambia and The Netherlands), Breel Embolo and Yvon Mvogo (Cameroon and Switzerland).

The contrast shows how African mobility is reshaping modern football not only by migration from Africa but by generations born and raised in Europe whose identities continue to bridge both continents.

It is within this complex ecosystem of aspiration and exploitation that Geoff operates. He is feckless and his sole objective is to sniff out undiscovered football talent with the help of Lefebvre, an experienced, semi-retired French scout.

For the French soccer agent Lefebvre, players like Eusébio were the earliest examples of the “Drogba Phenomenon,” in which African or Afro-descendant footballing youngsters, especially those with an immigrant profile like Marcel Desailly, born in Ghana, or Patrick Vieira, born in Senegal, became highly desirable in the global football market for their strength, skill, and technical adaptability shaped by exposure to different footballing environments.

Even today, many of the stars in the 2026 World Cup display the same characteristics: Sadio Mané’s rise from the renowned Senegalese academy Génération Foot or Amad Diallo’s Italian-Ivorian climb to Manchester United. Notably, some top players are just one generation removed from the continent — for example, Lamine Yamal’s roots in Equatorial Guinea and Morocco or Kylian Mbappé’s in Cameroon and Algeria.

Throughout Godwin, O’Neill navigates the transatlantic nature of youth football recruitment in Africa, inviting readers to trace their own historical connections to the relentless pursuit of new African talent.

Godwin also hints at a form of “footballing brain drain” in which some of Africa’s finest talents only achieve full recognition after entering European systems, akin to a primary resource reaching full potential only after undergoing refinement abroad.

At the event at GWU this past May, O’Neill underscored to students the “distinctly neocolonial dimension to this business of finding raw African talent.” As an example, he noted that metaphors used to describe African footballers – from Eusébio being dubbed A Pérola Negra (“The Black Pearl”) to agents “striking gold in Africa”– evoke a longer history of extraction on the continent that continues to be reflected in the structure of the modern football industry.

For O’Neill, the universality of football made it the most accessible medium to unravel this chaotic interplay. Speaking to students at George Washington University in Washington, DC, O’Neill admitted, “I learned English, psychology, history, geography, business, all on the football field.” Godwin’s characters also share the same curriculum generated on the pitch, yet the narrative suggests that, despite this shared classroom, its lessons can be interpreted and embodied in starkly different ways.

Lefebvre, the agent, repeatedly waffles on about his short-lived career and the recruitment dynamics behind some of African football’s greats. However, as the search for Godwin intensifies, O’Neill recounts the evocation of Treasure Island–like colonial literature, particularly through Lefebvre’s often disoriented and outsider view of certain African societies. Some of Lefebvre’s most passionate spiels on African youth football are tarnished by his retrograde notions about race, gender, geography, and culture. In one instance, Lefebvre justifies his caution while searching for Godwin’s team due to a fear of being misled by what he describes as the “African concept of truth,” where people say what is most profitable rather than following the European expectations of a promise or contract.

Lefebvre’s French identity is important as it places him as a holdover agent of the colonial era, responsible for moving resources from the périphérie to the metropole–in this case tracking down the elusive Godwin to deliver him to the European market. Lefebvre shepherds Wolfe through the hinterlands of West Africa in a Land Cruiser on a self-described “expedition” for Godwin. Lefebvre’s reductive tropes, often made through the backward lens of corruption and exploitation, such as in his description of an “African concept of truth,” echo a “colonial gaze” that still lingers over the modern-day sports industry in many African countries, where profit-driven recruiters pursue talent by any means necessary, creating a dangerous and illusory pathway for up-and-comers.
The parallels in Godwin to actual events are explicit.

Take the story of Cheikh Touré, an 18-year-old Senegalese goalkeeper lured to Ghana with the promise of a professional football trial to get to a European club. It turned out to be a fraudulent scheme. After his family was unable to pay the ransom to release him, Touré was tragically killed by the traffickers in October 2025 in Kumasi.
In 2024, several reports recount the stories of Kenyan, Nigerian, and Ghanaian footballers flown to Russia under false pretenses, to be subsequently deployed to the front lines in Ukraine.

Against this backdrop, the stories shared throughout Godwin – from Eusébio’s rise to European football glory to the Drogba Phenomenon – reveal the longer history O’Neill asks readers to confront: the enduring global pursuit of African talent with all its promise and peril. As already discovered African stars captivate World Cup audiences, attention will inevitably shift to where the next, yet unidentified, “Godwin-like” phenom will be found.

entry.summary: Joseph O’Neill’s new novel follows a Pittsburgh writer chasing a West African wonderkid. It’s also a story about who profits every time the world goes looking for the next Eusébio.

entry.title: Sovereign rot

div.p: In the heart of Ikoyi, Lagos, a fifteen-story concrete ghost haunts the skyline. The Old Federal Secretariat was once a nerve center of Nigerian power, functioning as the heart of Nigeria’s civil service. Since the federal capital was moved to Abuja in 1991, this complex has been left to rot. In a city defined by fervent construction and the relentless pursuit of newness, its stillness, frozen in time, is a provocation.

img.alt: Illustration of the abandoned Ikoyi Federal Secretariat in Lagos, a modernist high-rise complex rising above a dense foreground of bright green tree canopies.

div.p: Nigeria’s independence in 1960 arrived with serious ambition. Gifted by the British to mark the young nation’s sovereignty, the 25-story Independence Building served as the Republic’s first federal secretariat, anchoring the administrative machinery of the new state. As the civil service swelled during the oil boom years, the government erected the Ikoyi Secretariat in 1976. This new structure was designed to monumentalize the nation’s soaring aspirations — an architectural declaration that a young republic had outgrown its colonial infancy and entered a new era of industrial sophistication.

The Independence Building was eventually appropriated by the military and renamed Defence House. Today, it stands as a shadow of its former glory. Following a devastating fire in 1993, the military command abandoned the charred remains, relocating to the new capital of Abuja. Left behind in Lagos, the old tower’s narrow apertures now watch over the public square below like hollow eyes, stripped of its utility and its national significance.

Down the road, this architecture of abandonment reaches its literal peak at NECOM House. Built as the tallest skyscraper in the country, this telecommunications tower was conceived to be the crown jewel of the Lagos financial district; today, it suffers the same slow rot that plagues the civic landscape. This pattern of neglect repeats across the city center. Lagos is now a museum of deferred promises, littered with monumental structures left underused, suspended in time, or surrendered to decay.

The vacuum left by the government’s silent withdrawal from these sites has inevitably invited squatting and illicit activity. When the state refuses to occupy and maintain its landmarks while failing to provide housing, resources, and safety, it creates the conditions it then criminalizes. What appears as squalor is state neglect made visible. These buildings become shelter for those the state has rendered invisible. In a twist of irony, these administrative monuments have been involuntarily democratized.
While state-owned monoliths sit idle for decades, the government exhibits a violent agility elsewhere, bulldozing lives and properties in informal settlements with little to no prior notice.

Makoko, a historic community of roughly 100,000 residents, is one of Lagos’s most storied waterfront settlements. Established on the lagoon by the Egun fishing people, it has evolved over generations into a complex urban ecosystem built entirely on stilts. In December 2025, armed demolition teams backed by state authorities entered this settlement under the pretext of enforcing a safety corridor beneath a high-tension power line. Demolitions started two days before Christmas.

Over 3,000 homes, schools, and clinics were bulldozed and burned, displacing about 10,000 people. Protesters and civil society organizations have alleged that the demolitions resulted in deaths, including infants and elderly residents.

img.alt: Minimalist illustration of a lone figure standing in a small boat, using a long pole to propel it across still water against an otherwise empty white background.

figure.figcaption: Thousands were displaced just days before Christmas.

div.p: The official justification followed a familiar script: environmental concerns, urban renewal, the language of progress. But beneath the bureaucratic vocabulary, what it produced was displacement, lives dissolved into the water. In this context, the long-term abandonment of these spaces reads as an intentional pattern of uneven urgency. The government grants itself unlimited leniency regarding its own monumental dereliction, while displaying a ruthless impatience for the expedient improvisations of the people it has abandoned.

Deracination has shaped Lagos’s socio-economic fabric for generations, and the map of the city can serve as a historical record of state-led displacement. Take Obalende, whose name translates to “the [British] king chased us here” — an etymology the historian K. Dike traced, in a 1997 Guardian essay, to the colonial army’s expansion into the area. Today, it is a bustling hub bordering Lagos Island, but its origins trace back to the colonial era, when the British crown displaced the local population in favor of expanding an army base. This is a foundational precedent of spatial injustice that outlived the empire. Instead of dismantling this colonial architecture of exclusion, the modern Nigerian state has embraced and optimized it, expressing its sovereign authority through the violence of forcible land clearance rather than the duty of housing its most vulnerable communities.

The message to the average Lagosian is clear: Space is scarce when it belongs to the poor, expendable when it belongs to the state, and available to those with enough clout to bend the city to their will. When there is corporate capital to secure or elite enclaves to engineer, the state magically rediscovers its capacity for urban planning. Ultimately, the rotting high-rises of the Marina and the demolished stilt-houses of Makoko are symptoms of the same institutional disease. They represent a state that has fundamentally abdicated its social contract, leaving behind a city that is simultaneously starved for public life and choked by avarice.

For those tasked with shaping the built environment, this landscape of sovereign rot poses a sharp ethical challenge. We are trained to obsess over the new, chasing the next “smart city.” But what does it mean to design for the future in a city where the most basic act of care — maintenance — has been undervalued by those meant to uphold it the most?

To answer this is to confront a notoriously wicked problem, an entangled crisis in which the professional domains of the architect, the policymaker, and the developer are all implicated. In Braiding Sweetgrass, Robin Wall Kimmerer notes a sobering truth: “As the land becomes impoverished, so too does the scope of [our] vision.” Lagos, and indeed much of Nigeria, suffers acutely from this exact starvation of perspective. On paper, the mechanics of urban revitalization are not rocket science. However, the unchecked greed permitted to fester across the country has corroded the foundations of every civic institution and shriveled the imagination of our city-makers.

When presented with decades of water-adapted vernacular literacy in Makoko, or the complex maritime history of Tarkwa Bay, the developer’s only legible response is demolition — flattening centuries of ecological resilience to install a yacht club or a generic “luxury” tower. This impoverished vision can only copy; it cannot synthesize. It views indigenous knowledge as a blight to be cleared and abandoned structures as dead weight, all while funding exclusive archipelagos reclaimed from the sea. Eko Atlantic stands as the ultimate expression of this hubris: a private enclave engineered for the few, rising from the ocean while the waterfront communities of the many are erased to make room for the supply chain of exclusivity.

By chasing the illusion of the “blank slate,” the architect becomes the aesthetic enforcement arm of this system, providing the glossy renders that legitimize spatial violence long before the bulldozers arrive. The policymaker completes the triangle. It is the state that issues the demolition orders, absorbs the legal challenges, and quietly steps aside for the developer. The FBT Coral Estate agreement, in which the Lagos State Government negotiated a 25 percent stake in the “luxury” development designed to replace Makoko, exemplifies this arrangement explicitly. Everything is transactional.
By trading the social contract for a real estate ledger, the state has rendered its own history meaningless and its people invisible. Lagos continues to rise, but it rises against itself.

The abandoned Secretariat and the state-sanctioned displacement are evidence of a system functioning exactly as those who benefit from it intend. “Smart city” rhetoric and urban renewal frameworks create the assumption of a state that has lost its way, merely requiring the right policy intervention to find its footing again. But a government that can mobilize armed demolition teams against impoverished communities two days before Christmas, while its own civic infrastructure crumbles unremarked across the city, has not lost its way. It has chosen one.

entry.summary: From Eko Atlantic to the Niger Delta, elite enclaves have become the defining spatial expression of Nigeria’s political order.

entry.title: Had he been buried

div.p: They came seeking solitude in a private family graveyard in our common neighborhood in Riruta, a suburb of Nairobi City, around mid-morning towards the end of September 2018. I was already there. My weakening eyesight could make out only images of two adults.
This is private land. They could be the owners of the land, I thought to myself.
I waved at them rapidly. They both waved back. I walked towards them.
“Oooh! So it’s you!” I exclaimed. These were not the owners of the land and the graveyard after all. It was Binyavanga Wainaina and his helper.
“You two know each other?” his helper asked.
“Of course!” I replied.

Binyavanga had changed a great deal since I had last seen him. The multiple strokes had severely incapacitated him. His speech came out in an agonizing slur. I tried to ease his discomfort by speaking more, compensating for his forced silence.
“Such vast private lands are uncommon in this city,” I observed. “In fact, they are abominable and unjustifiable in a metropolis like Nairobi bursting with deprived humanity.”
He nodded repeatedly in agreement.

There was a huge fig tree on the land. In African spirituality, the fig tree is sacred. Among the Agikuyu people, it is known as Mugumo. Our people once worshipped and offered sacrifices beneath Mugumo trees. We walked closer to it. Its enormous trunk was hollow, forming something like a passageway through the middle. I walked in and out of the trunk the way we used to do in our childhood among the giant podo trees along River Nanyuki. This particular Mugumo was immense, tall, wide, and commanding. Its huge branches spread outward like a canopy over a vast area.
“A Mugumo is never pruned,” one of the owners of that land had once told me casually. “Cutting it is sacrilegious and cursed.”

Such a sacred tree was best left alone, I thought to myself. It was an abode of ancestral spirits. But wait — as children, we had been warned never to walk seven times around a Mugumo. Boys, we were told, would turn into girls, and girls into boys. We did. Nothing happened. It was a myth, an old tale that could not contain the free and wandering spirits of our childhood. I had walked several times around this particular Mugumo in the neighborhood and I remained who I was. I felt only solace and solitude as I escaped into my inner self.

We held animated conversations beside the Mugumo for a long while, hardly noticing the passage of time. We spoke about literature, religion, politics, creative writing, African liberation, Mau Mau, Mwakenya, Kwani?, dreams, life, survival of artists, hope, and much more. Mwakenya was the underground socialist movement of the 1980s in Kenya whose members and supporters were brutally suppressed by the Moi–KANU dictatorship. Kwani? is the literary magazine Binyavanga co-founded in 2003 with his Caine Prize winnings, which became the crucible of a new generation of Kenyan and African writing.

Binyavanga barely spoke, his words still slurred, yet he nodded excitedly and often in agreement. His helper listened attentively. Meanwhile, I spoke endlessly, releasing words like a newly activated word processor.

I first met Binyavanga Wainaina in 2002 at a shopping mall in Nairobi during the Nairobi International Book Fair. He had just won the Caine Prize for African Writing. Literary excitement was palpable among the country’s literati. Fresh literary flowers had sprouted, blossoming with beauty and releasing a sweet fragrance, new expressions, new voices; a generation emerging from relative obscurity, as Frantz Fanon had prophesied, either to fulfill its mission or betray it.

Binyavanga was one of the key speakers at the opening ceremony of the book fair. He spoke eloquently about new and vibrant literary horizons and renewed hope in the country. Names such as Nameless, Kalamashaka, Ukoo Flani Mau Mau, some of the hip hop artists then dominating the musical airwaves, rolled effortlessly from his tongue like a staccato burst from a machine gun. In many ways, he himself was a literary machine gun.
“Why are we still trapped in old narratives about the past glory of African literature as if nothing new is happening?” he asked.
Why Are We So Blest? I recalled in the same breath the title of the novel by Ayi Kwei Armah.

Loud applause followed his speech, just as it was echoing across other literary and artistic spaces and sites in the country: Kenya National Theatre, Club Soundd, the GoDown Arts Centre, Sarakasi Dome, Kuona Trust, Kwani LitFest, a lot more.
We met again in 2004 at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi during the Kenya Social Forum. He lingered at the back of the largely activist crowd. I thought he cut a somewhat forlorn figure.

“Another Kenya Is Possible” was the theme of the forum, attuned to the global call of the World Social Forum: “Another World Is Possible.” The local and global processes of the World Social Forum sought to locate and connect people’s struggles for a just world. Politics, we argued, must secure livelihoods. We spoke of climate justice, not merely the language of climate change. We spoke about struggles for food sovereignty, not simply food security. The earth was being decimated by capitalist greed. Soulless corporations, placing profits before people’s welfare, were driving the world towards the brink of extinction. Our world was dying. Progressive forces everywhere needed urgently to coalesce.

Binyavanga at some point later on wrote a post on how hard he had tried to be socialist “as a person of good conscience.” He observed that to many people, “progressive” meant being a socialist. He wanted to be “progressive,” but also believed that the fall of the left globally was real and that the left was fatally flawed. He believed we are in the era of the perfection of capitalism and that capitalism was the best way out for what he considered to be Africa’s century.
I differed with him on his faith in capitalism. I believe capitalism is a mortal disaster for humankind, and that socialism remains the alternative.

But we agreed on the centrality of literature. Literature does not merely fuel struggle; it is itself a vehicle of people’s struggles for freedoms and liberation. That was why we were at the event of the Kenya Social Forum — to locate literature within progressive awakenings, away from the cacophony of tribal politics in the country and the wastelands of art for art’s sake.
We exchanged contacts.
“I will send you the manuscript of my novel,” I promised.
“Sawa!” he said excitedly.

He left shortly afterwards. I remained. The Kenya Social Forum would continue for three more days, and I would stay throughout to help coordinate the event. I was happy to witness sites and spaces of people’s struggles for emancipation taking shape and getting grounded. The arts are the high priests of people’s struggles. Literature is their bishop.
I truly wanted to share with Binyavanga the manuscript of my novel. I never did. My life, like his, was then like a flickering candle in the wind.

We walked to the private family graveyard near the Mugumo tree. Graves of several members of the family that owned the land were located there. Binyavanga stood transfixed before one grave in particular. It belonged to a senior colonial chief who had once ruled this area on behalf of the colonial regime. The tragedy of the chief’s betrayal and treachery had finally come to this: a grave covered by mounds of soil and concrete.

I tried to read his gaze in my mind. The chief’s true legacy, I thought, was one of servitude to colonial masters and betrayal of his own people. I nodded inwardly. Traitors who sold their souls in pursuit of hollow glory, passing comforts, and obscene wealth. The tragedy of colonial betrayal still haunts this country and many other neocolonial states. But death remains the great equalizer for us all.

Binyavanga kept his eyes fixed on the graves for a long while. I wondered whether his mind was wandering as deeply as mine. Our gazes seemed both psychic and spiritual. My thoughts admonished me: So this is what most lives are finally reduced to — skeletons beneath the pride of flesh, memorial plaques bearing dates of birth and death, reminders of the vanity of human existence.
“Vanity of vanities; all is vanity,” says the Preacher in the Bible. “It is like chasing after the wind.”

For most of us, the graveyard is the final destination. Death humbles life. Death should compel us to reflect continually on the meaning and purpose of our existence. In the end, the memory of our lives either fades like passing clouds or endures like seeds that nourish future generations. Such is karma.

The mortal remains of the colonial chief lay in that graveyard discarded and reviled by many. His memory and that of his kind in the betrayal and treachery to the people only helps to fuel people’s struggles for a just society. The generational wealth and privilege inherited from colonial treachery may have survived him, but they too shall one day pass away.
Soon.
