I later invited him and his helper to our apartment nearby. He touched the books on the bookshelf as though they were living spirits. In a real sense, books are the abodes of their writers, spirits in themselves, words made flesh and memory. I pulled from the bookshelf several of his works, one after another: Discovering Home; How to Write About Africa; One Day I Will Write About This Place; Beyond River Yei.

His face lit up instantly. His eyes moved, mesmerized, from the books to the bookshelf and back again. I could see his joy, his calmness, his deep sense of comfort. His eyes seemed to say aloud: There lies my literary legacy.
We later walked to his apartment along the main road. We lived in a working-class suburb. Nearby was a sprawling slum.
“I like it here more than anywhere else I have lived,” he told me as we entered his apartment.

The living room was furnished with antique pieces that gave the space both a traditional and modern feel. His MacBook laptop appeared to be the most modern treasure in the room. He strained his eyes while reading and typing; his eyesight was weakening. So was mine. I can no longer see distant objects clearly without glasses. I was not sure whether he owned a pair of reading glasses.
He showed me his bedroom. It was a tidy mess. Books lay everywhere, exciting titles, mostly fiction and creative nonfiction. Some had been gifts from friends.
“Pick any you may want,” he told me.

I was tempted to take A Brief History of Seven Killings by Marlon James. But I did not. I thought I would pick it later. I did not even pick it up when we returned afterwards. Some books carry spirits better left to haunt their authors and owners.

We then headed for a rendezvous at Dagoretti Corner. We partook of lots of nyama choma and mutura, washed down with drinks and laughter wrapped in silence. Nyama choma is grilled meat, and mutura is a Kenyan sausage; both are staples of Nairobi’s social eating. We spoke nothing there of our pet talks on literature, African liberation, African spirituality, and such heavy topics, choosing instead to relish our food and drinks in measured quietness. Outside, along the main road beyond the restaurant, weary laboring masses trudged home from the daily drudgery of sustaining this unequal country and materialist society.

As evening reached its climax and darkness descended, we moved to Dagoz Artists Bar close by for a night of live music. The space was tiny and intimate. The artists performing on the main stage were as much part of the revelry as the audience itself. Anyone with a voice could burst into song, however coarse or unpolished. The main stage was within reach of everyone inside, part of the collective repertoire. Our table, like the others nearby, seemed almost an extension of the stage itself.

We bellowed out the words of our favorite songs alongside the performers, shouting ourselves hoarse in the attempt. The din of drunken voices and clashing sounds was an exercise in glorious discordance. Loud talk and shouting seemed the only acceptable means of communication there; quiet conversations were out of place. The cacophony of voices and sounds beat like a riot of sound, yet somehow it grounded our solitude and tethered our restless artistic spirits to a sense of order.

The music went on even after the session artists had left the stage. We could still hear it from outside as we departed singing along. We drove back with the rhythms and voices still drumming through our minds, soothing us into the calm of the night and into deep sleep.

Binyavanga returned another day to the private family graveyard, this time alone. From a distance, I saw him standing transfixed, staring at the grave of the colonial chief. I thought perhaps his spirituality was reawakening in ways he himself could no longer clearly express in his condition. He had once written about his spiritual Sangoma in South Africa who had advised him to return home and honor his rich ancestral lineage.

He called it African spirituality. I understood it, too, as a return to the roots of African civilization — back to narratives of African victories, not merely of conquest and defeat; back to multiple African narratives. Narratives of order, dignity, and peace before slavery and colonialism. Narratives that ask difficult questions: Why were we enslaved? Why were we colonized? Why do we continue allowing ourselves to be recolonized?

No wonder the Mugumo tree occupies such sacred importance in the spirituality of the Agikuyu people. It defies both time and territory. It is said that the Mugumo under which Dedan Kimathi worshipped in the forest while leading the Mau Mau war for independence in Kenya fell soon after his capture by colonial forces. Dedan Kimathi was the field marshal of the Kenya Land and Freedom Army popularly known as Mau Mau. He was captured in 1956 and executed by the British colonial regime in 1957. Indigenous trees are living connections to our spirituality, to our ways of being, to memory and identity.
Wangari Maathai came to mind, embracing a huge tree in her struggle for ecological justice. The graveyard, too, spoke of return, going back to the soil, forever nourishing Mother Earth.
“For dust you are, and to dust you shall return,” the priest at the Catholic church across the main road often intoned from the Bible at the beginning of the Lenten season.

African spirituality converges with the sanctity of the soil, replenishing our lives. Our existence moving endlessly in cycles of birth and death; birth and death again, the eternal rhythms of earthly life. Why trouble yourself? Why worry? I thought Binyavanga’s Sangoma would have rejoiced.

I walked back with Binyavanga to his apartment, somehow feeling revitalized. He too seemed renewed, especially in the way we both jovially greeted folks in our neighborhood, most of them only casual acquaintances. His generosity and capacity for love were legendary in many ways. The doors of his heart were wide open to anyone capable of being loved. “Could you be loved,” Bob Marley would sing of such spirits. Binyavanga’s helper could attest to this.

At some point, Binyavanga received funds from his family’s inheritance. I accompanied him to the office of his family’s lawyer in Westlands area in Nairobi to sign documents releasing the inheritance. He had mentioned that the lawyer’s office was near a Mugumo tree in Westlands. I had never imagined that such a sacred fig tree still existed within the city. I do not know whether it is still there today.

Later, I accompanied him and his helper to his bank in the Karen area of Nairobi. I believed he transferred a decent sum of the funds to some of his close friends and a lover. Once Binyavanga’s heart and mind settled on something he wanted, he became stubbornly resistant to caution or advice.

He seemed to have got a decent amount from the inheritance. He inquired about investments in land to settle among his close friends near Nairobi National Park. He dreamed of building there a beautiful villa attuned to his tastes, blending antique elegance with modern architecture. I was of little help in matters of land investment. I could neither advise him nor claim any experience of my own in such matters.

I was not able to accompany him and his helper later that evening for dinner and an outing at a top high-end hotel in the city. They bought lots of exquisite items at the hotel that night. In a rush to please his helper, Binyavanga bought him a pair of expensive leather boots late at night. They discovered the following day that the pair of boots were mismatched. He would often give his helper his ATM card to withdraw cash for him. Many times, I was worried that his generosity might someday be taken advantage of, and that the helper might disappear on him. I suspect that this eventually happened, when his helper switched off his phone and vanished from contact altogether. I have neither seen nor heard from him ever since.
We shared several wishes between us. Binyavanga spoke of his desire to learn the Dholuo language.
“That might be too late now,” I said.
“Nooo!” he replied, gesturing emphatically in disagreement with my incredulity. I noticed that his calmness and joy were beginning to fade, and I quickly corrected myself in jest.
“At least for me. I have almost given up the effort of learning another language. Another of my wishes is learning to play the guitar. Another is to swim without a floater.” He giggled.
There were many unfulfilled wishes within us. Binyavanga’s age and mine were already nearing the halfway mark toward the sunset of our lives.

But you have achieved more for African literature in such a short time. You have truly lived your life. I did not say these words aloud. I was speaking to myself. He might have mistaken them for flattery. He was often a pace-setter, bubbling with ideas and projects that others eventually fulfilled. I suppose that is how legacy and heritage are secured.
“Asante!” I told him.
He looked at me intensely, struggling to express himself.
“Thank you too,” he said, his slurred words carrying a deep inner turmoil.

I could feel his frustration at being unable to communicate effectively. It was uncharacteristic of the man who in the recent past had dazzled audiences with eloquent speeches. But I am a believer that better and brighter days are still ahead of us. I downloaded an online guidebook by the Stroke Association: Helping Someone with Communication Problems — Together We Can Conquer Stroke. I promised myself that in the days ahead I would read it carefully and learn how better to communicate with him. I never did. Another of my wishes quietly passed away.
I was away on work outside the city for about three weeks. Around the same time, Binyavanga had traveled to Rwanda for the burial of an uncle. When we both returned, we somehow failed to reconnect.
“He has traveled to the coast for a vacation,” his nurse told me.

He remained vibrant on social media throughout the trip. I followed him mostly on Facebook, where he posted photographs of himself and his companion strolling leisurely along the shores of the Indian Ocean, staying at one of the luxurious hotels on the Kenyan coast. The pictures showed his efforts to remain calm, joyful, and at peace with himself, living life as fully as he could despite his failing health.

I imagined the other escapades they might have engaged in at the coast. They would don safety gear before hopping onto a speedboat, floaters fastened reassuringly around them. The boat would surge into the deep sea, rising and plunging against the huge waves as they exclaimed in fear, awe, and excitement. Then a dolphin would suddenly leap out of the water in a graceful somersault. Another would follow, then another, until several dolphins were performing what seemed like a perfectly choreographed spectacle. Aware perhaps of the human gaze upon them, the creatures would intensify their display. Dolphins, it is said, are among the cleverest creatures in the sea. One would leap, then another, and another still, their performance lingering until the speedboats disappeared into the horizon.

They might also have witnessed another spectacle, this time closer to the shore. Snorkeling through the shallow waters, they would see countless small marine creatures crawling and drifting beneath the surface, dazzling in every imaginable color, shape, and pattern. The experience would have been immaculate, a refreshing bliss. We should crown such stories with a cold beer when we meet again, I wished.

But that wish, too, never came to pass. Shortly afterwards, his health deteriorated and he was hospitalized. I visited him at the hospital a few times. Access to him there remained largely a private family affair, limited to a handful of close friends. We did not see much of each other again.
I was later away in Johannesburg for a period of further studies.
“I love Johannesburg,” he had once told me during one of our conversations. “I would like to buy a house there. I love the vibe and spirit of that city, a city for free spirits.”

I often moved around in Johannesburg, or Joburg, as it is fondly called. I met friends he would have loved to meet. I saw and lived in houses and estates that would have suited his tastes. I wandered through art galleries and bookshops he would have lingered in for hours. I attended jazz sessions and absorbed the loves and contradictions of that vibrant city, perhaps much as he would have done himself. I listened to fiery discussions on African liberation politics, subjects he followed with keen interest. In more ways than I could imagine, Binyavanga accompanied my thoughts throughout my stay there.
Clues of the sad news first came through a missed call from Isaac, our mutual friend and one of Binyavanga’s closest companions. I called him back, but there was no answer.
I grew disturbed. Why would Isaac call so unusually early?

Shortly afterwards, I read the news. Binyavanga had passed away. He had been frail and ailing, but I had hoped he would prevail, as he had triumphed in so many other battles before. The literary world still looked forward to his boisterous spirit, his gregarious presence, and the boundless imagination that helped spark a literary renaissance in our country, across Africa, and within international literary circles. Death does not equalize such souls. His spirit had already triumphed.

“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” The priest at the Catholic church across the main road in our suburb often recited this line from the Bible for souls such as his.

From Johannesburg, I followed online the celebration of Binyavanga’s life at the Kenya National Theatre, where family, friends, and hordes of admirers gathered not in grief alone, but in affirmation of the immense spirit he had shared with the world.
“We must free our imaginations,” he had urged in one of his final videos. “Celebrate my life. Do not mourn me,” he had also declared boldly on Facebook.

Binyavanga was cremated in a private ceremony. At the time, I did not fully grasp the significance of that final act, but over the years, I have often found myself wondering: Would he have wanted his mortal remains laid to rest in a graveyard? When he would return to the private family graveyard in our shared neighborhood and stand there for long moments, transfixed by the graves before him, was he contemplating the physical form of legacy and remembrance? Would he have preferred a gravesite where his many admirers, friends, and fans would gather to pay their respects? Perhaps. Perhaps not. His family and those closest to him knew better.

What matters most is that his spirit endures, in memory, in literature, and in the enduring company of remarkable African writers who refuse oblivion. Though his body returned to ashes, his words continue to breathe among us.
Had he been buried, I might have proposed his epitaph, borrowed from the Italian writer Oriana Fallaci:

blockquote.p: To write is to die a little less when I die, to leave the children I did not have, to make people think a little more.

div.p: I recently returned to our shared neighborhood. The private family graveyard is still there. The remains of the colonial chief still lies beneath his slab of concrete, his name and dates fixed into stone, reviled, unvisited, and largely forgotten, while Binyavanga, who has no grave at all. is visited every day by readers across the world who pull his books from their shelves, as I still pull them from mine. His resting place was never a graveyard. It was always language.

The Mugumo still stands, unpruned and sacred, its hollow trunk opening like a doorway between worlds, the living and the ancestral. Some spirits require no grave to mark where they rest. They live in stories, in words, and in the quiet defiance of memory.

entry.summary: Binyavanga Wainaina was cremated in a private ceremony in 2019. In his final year, the writer kept returning to a colonial chief’s grave beneath a sacred fig tree in Nairobi — as if contemplating what remains of a life.

entry.title: Is football still capable of scandal?

div.p: Virginia Giuffre, Annie Farmer, Chauntae Davis, Jesse Michaels, and countless other women and girls were part of an international scandal that captured the public imagination in ways never seen before. And yet their names were barely mentioned. Earlier in the year, there was furious demand for the list of powerful men implicated in the Epstein files from all ends of the political spectrum. And the interest wasn’t just tied to the crimes themselves; it carried the hope that the exposure of the most visible and wealthy men in the world would lead to a reckoning akin to the #MeToo movement. What is implicit in this hope is that if there is accountability at the highest levels, then there would be a trickle-down effect that could assist in confronting the more quotidian and less publicized violence.
What the Epstein files made clear is that there is a distinction between society’s stated moral values and how those values are lived out.

However, that did not transpire. What did happen was the files turned into a spectacle. The anticipation for them, their release, their dissection, the jokes in between, the aftermath. And somewhere along the line, the victims were moved out of sight. Then people moved on. The focus shifted from the files to an ill-advised war against Iran, a green pool in the US capital, and the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

The period between the end of the World Cup and the start of club European football presents an opportunity to reflect on the tournament and all the events and discussions that occurred. One of the conversations that briefly captured the footballing community was the allegations of sexual misconduct against several footballers. Thomas Partey and Achraf Hakimi are facing pending criminal trials, Ryan Mendes remains under active police investigation, while players such as Junya Ito, Kaishu Sano, Andreas Schjelderup, Thiago Almada, and Cristiano Ronaldo have all seen their cases reach their legal conclusions.

These stories did not offer new revelations. But an update on the status of Hakimi’s case, as well as Canada’s refusal to approve Partey’s visa application, summoned the ghosts that have long haunted football.

FIFA, national federations, coaches, teammates, and media deferred to legality, recruiting the criminal justice system as a kind of Big Other, the final arbiter of truth, despite the awareness of its shortcomings and limitations. This is most clearly demonstrated in how the courts are tasked with providing assurances and resolving ethical questions that exceed their mandate of due process. In the interim, innocence was not only presumed; it was asserted.

And while there is a subset of the public that abides by this logic, it does not fully capture the rest of the football ecosystem. Many supporters expressed genuine anger and were vehemently advocating for the removal of these players from their teams. But as soon as the whistle blew, that indignation was muffled. And 90 minutes later, there was discourse around tactics, ref calls, VAR, substitutions, etc.
It raises the question: if there is enough consensus, why isn’t there coordination? What is it about football that allows us to know and yet continue as though we did not?
And the most curious of all, what if outrage is part of the entertainment?
Any answer has to begin with understanding the power of images. Jacques Lacan argues that human beings understand themselves and the world through the symbolic order.

Football is an image-making factory. The fancy footwork, the immaculate touches, the bicycle kicks, and the extra-time winners aren’t just about sublime technique. They become repositories through which spectators organize their ideas, desires, and fears. It is through the moments of magic in which fans come to identify with clubs, countries, and versions of themselves.

In Society of the Spectacle, Guy Debord furthers this point: ours is an age that prefers the sign to the thing itself, the copy to the original, appearance to essence — one in which, as he puts it, “truth is considered profane, and only illusion is sacred.”

So when the reality of rape accusations, FIFA’s corruption, capitalism, imperialism, racism, and labor exploitation threaten to rupture that “sacredness,” audiences respond with real moral outrage, but that rarely converts into sustained pressure. The viewer learns to live with the contradiction without allowing it to reorganize their participation. And this happens not necessarily to protect the players or FIFA per se, but to protect the enjoyment they produce.

That is how the story of Cape Verde became one of the underdog, of extraordinary heroics that transformed them into Africa’s footballing fairytale, and not one of a squad that fielded a player under investigation for rape.

That is how the story of Norway became one of history in the making, of Erling Haaland’s charisma and imaginary Viking boats rowing into the quarterfinals, and not one of a team that harbored a convicted sex offender.
That is how the story of Japan became one of model discipline and cleanliness in the stadium and in the locker room, and not the fact that they have two players accused of sexual assault.

This dynamic is not limited to sexual violence. Football has developed a remarkable capacity to move from one moral crisis to the next and absorb the scandals along the way. During this tournament, the focus shifted from the unfair treatment of the Iranian team to visa denials to the Balogun controversy and countless other flashpoints. The previous tournament revolved around Qatar’s labor exploitation, worker conditions, migrant deaths, and FIFA’s corruption. A similar pattern happens on a club level with incidents of racism, financial irregularities, and controversial sponsorships. Each issue, different in stakes and complexity, is treated the same. They command intense attention until something else happens.

But the issues themselves don’t disappear; they are temporarily suspended from collective consciousness until they get recycled again. Like the Epstein files, the condemnation they provoke becomes part of the spectacle itself. It is very predictable in its life cycle and its outcomes. Ultimately, the problems are not adequately addressed. It’s like a choreographed dance.

And when it comes to sexual crimes, audiences think of themselves as ambidextrous — that they are capable of taking the allegations seriously and enjoying the football, as if the two aren’t in conversation with one another. And unfortunately, spectacles of this nature have a tendency toward erasure. The victims are not only pushed to the background but they are almost rendered invisible. No names, no faces, and no specific stories. They are treated as placeholders and their lives are reduced to legal cases and another talking point.

MeToo was neither perfect nor immune from the dynamics of spectacle. It was introduced to the world through the experiences of famous, rich, white women, which overshadowed the grassroots work that the organization does on the ground. And because of the spectacle, it exists in the public imagination as an era and not a continuous movement that empowers victims to come forward with their stories. However, what distinguished it from a movement like Time’s Up is that it didn’t organize around what punishment perpetrators should receive; it dedicated attention to the agency and care of victims and survivors.

It did not hand over ethical responsibility to the courts, as it understood that courts are not designed to do that in the first place. Instead, moral duty was distributed across the larger social world. Sometimes convictions followed; oftentimes they did not. Some perpetrators lost their reputations while others lost their influence. Yet the movement’s ambitions never depended on those outcomes alone. It also created the conditions in which victims were no longer expected to remain invisible while institutions deliberated the fate of those who had harmed them.

The movement also offered pathways for restoration. After Megan Ganz publicly described the sexual harassment she experienced working for Dan Harmon as a writer for Community, the public discourse gave the two of them an opportunity to engage in dialogue, and Harmon responded with a sincere and rare apology to atone for his actions.

Returning to football, if the sport has ritualized outrage and the institutions can shrug it off, then the solution cannot be found in producing more outrage. Right now, discussions circulate around the idea of whether players should be allowed to play instead of considering why that has become the only point of inquiry.

The other instinctive response is often a boycott. But boycotting isn’t always the most practical or transformative solution. Sometimes it does the reverse of what it intends, and it can offer an easy way out. As mentioned earlier, football is entangled with so many emotional and psychic investments, and therefore boycotting as a political strategy will have the mammoth task of trying to get buy-in before it can even challenge institutions.

Placing steady pressure on FIFA and federations to develop a player policy is a worthy cause. However, it is also one that lends itself to institutional failure. It is a tough ask to demand that organizations properly adjudicate the conduct of their money-makers. It’s limping before it can be put to the test.

None of these interventions should be abandoned; they just cannot be exhaustive. Any solution should consider preventative measures and a different framework of engagement rather than being narrow and reactive. In fact, any intervention will have limitations. Football is deeply embedded within patriarchal structures, and eradicating the violence it produces ultimately requires a complete overhaul of gendered and racial hierarchies. That is not happening today, nor tomorrow, and it is unlikely that it will happen in this lifetime. But it doesn’t mean that reforms are meaningless or can’t produce measurable outcomes.
So the challenge is not to create a football free of contradiction but to interrupt the rituals that allow contradictions to become ordinary. That requires asking better questions.
How can football shift its attention toward victims without reducing them to spectacle?
What would collective action among the fans look like with this in mind?
And finally, what does accountability look like beyond waiting for FIFA or the criminal justice system to act?

entry.summary: From the Epstein files to a World Cup trailed by rape charges and a hush-money settlement, the public has gotten remarkably good at feeling outrage. What it hasn’t learned is what to do with it.

entry.title: The grid inside the grid

div.p: In March, when Cassava Technologies announced the launch of an AI factory powered by NVIDIA in South Africa, the company described it as a turning point. African businesses would gain local access to high-performance computing. Data would remain within African borders. Developers would be able to build models for local languages and local problems.

The promise matters. African researchers and firms cannot participate meaningfully in artificial intelligence if they must rent every unit of computing power from servers abroad. But the most consequential infrastructure inside an AI factory may not be the graphics processor. It may be the electricity connection.

Artificial intelligence is exceptionally energy hungry. The International Energy Agency expects global electricity consumption by data centers to nearly double by 2030. The pressure is not evenly distributed. Data centers cluster in particular cities and industrial corridors, where their demand can collide with already constrained transmission systems.

South Africa shows how this collision is being managed. Data center operators are increasingly securing electricity through private renewable plants and wheeling arrangements, which allow power generated in one province to travel across the national network to a customer elsewhere. Teraco, a major operator, is developing a 120-megawatt solar plant in the Free State to supply its facilities in Johannesburg and Cape Town. Other operators have signed similar agreements.

This can look like responsible investment. Private procurement adds renewable generation, reduces dependence on coal, and helps large customers avoid drawing all their electricity from local distribution networks. South Africa’s electricity supply has also improved after years of blackouts. Yet the country still needs to expand and strengthen its transmission network. A private solar farm does not create a private route from the sun to a server. It still depends on substations, power lines, and grid capacity financed and governed as part of the national system.

The concern is not abstract. In May, community organizations challenged plans for two Equinix data centers in Cape Town, arguing that the applications did not provide enough information about electricity demand, water use, emissions, and backup power. The proposed facilities could require up to 160 megawatts combined. The dispute asks a basic democratic question: How should cities weigh private digital investment against competing claims on shared resources?

This is the grid inside the grid: a layer of firm, privately secured electricity built for facilities that cannot tolerate interruption, operating within a public system still struggling to expand transmission and connect new generation. The AI factory may be geographically located in South Africa, but its relationship to the surrounding economy can resemble an enclave. It receives dedicated power, imported equipment, sophisticated cooling, and backup generation. The wider public is promised future innovation, jobs, and growth.

The same tension is visible in Kenya. A proposed $1 billion data center involving Microsoft and the Emirati company G42 was presented as a geothermal-powered foundation for East Africa’s cloud and AI economy. By May 2026, negotiations had stalled over requests for guaranteed capacity payments, while the scale of the project’s power requirements remained under discussion. The episode revealed what investment announcements often conceal: Governments may be asked not only to host digital infrastructure but also to guarantee its market and reorganize scarce energy capacity around it.

None of this means African governments should reject data centers. Local computing capacity can reduce latency, support universities and startups, keep sensitive data closer to home, and create alternatives to total dependence on overseas cloud regions. The issue is not whether AI infrastructure should be built. It is whether public systems become stronger because it is built.

That requires more than celebratory language about sovereignty. Governments should disclose the electricity, water, land, tax, and guarantee arrangements attached to large data center projects. New power procurement should demonstrate that it adds generation rather than simply reserving existing transmission capacity. Contracts should require investment in shared grid infrastructure, meaningful local access to computing resources, and credible plans for skills and research partnerships. Backup diesel use and environmental impacts should be visible rather than buried in technical filings.

Sovereign AI cannot mean that data remain inside national borders while the infrastructure around them becomes inaccessible to the society hosting it. The real test is simpler: After the servers are switched on, is there more power, more capacity, and more public value than there was before?

entry.summary: Africa’s new AI factories promise digital sovereignty. Their electricity deals may instead create private power islands inside public systems.

entry.title: Africa’s last philosopher king

div.p: Nelson Mandela, the first democratic president of South Africa (1994–1999), secured a catalytic and at times confounding place in world history. He was neither an enthralling orator, an imposing Great Man, nor a formidable intellectual. Yet his birthday, July 18, has been marked by the United Nations as “Nelson Mandela International Day.” He is the only former head of state in contemporary times to enjoy such transnational iconic status. Here, I claim that his unique place in history can be explained by how closely he resembles a philosopher king.

The “philosopher king” or “philosopher ruler” is a western philosophy concept that originates in the following claim by Greek philosopher Socrates, found in his mentee Plato’s book The Republic: “The human race will have no respite from evils until those who are really philosophers acquire political power or until, through some divine dispensation, those who rule and have political authority in the cities become real philosophers.”

South African philosopher Mabogo Percy More adds that a philosopher is not only a scholar of the subject, but also “an individual who has the capacity to make an original contribution to the development of philosophical thought and to the world of ideas irrespective of his [her] training in the discipline.”

Although the concept referred to state rule by the monarchy or aristocracy when The Republic was written (between 380 and 375 BCE), in contemporary democratic politics the term is not used literally. It has come to refer to heads of state such as presidents, prime ministers, and chancellors, as well as the remaining monarchs. It simultaneously captures the Janusian contradiction of an ideal form of rational and ethical leadership (the philosophical element) and a caution of autocratic leadership (the king, ruler, or political element).

Africa’s first post-independence heads of state, also referred to as “Africa’s Founding Fathers,” were conferred this mantle because they were not only political leaders but also thought leaders. Political scholar Vusi Gumede asserts that a “thought leader is someone who possesses the right kind of knowledge needed to challenge an existing paradigm in order to advance new thinking and to inspire others as well.” They challenged Western imperialist and colonial paradigms.

Despite their flaws, Africa’s Founding Fathers became beacons of inspiration for their people during the euphoric era of independence and decolonization. Collectively, as Africa’s philosopher kings, they formulated or promoted theories and concepts, delivered eloquent speeches, and wrote influential works pertaining to African communalism, African nationalism, African socialism, Afrocentrism, Négritude, Nkrumaism, Consciencism, and Ujamaa.

South Africa is a unique outlier in this landscape. After the colonial settlement of the Dutch from the 17th century — predating the European Scramble for Africa (1880–1914) — together with Britain’s colonial stake in the late 19th century, the country endured a further four decades of white minority, Afrikaner nationalist, and apartheid (separate development) rule. Thus, South Africa’s liberation was only realized in 1994.

Hence, Mandela became the last 20th-century post-independence leader on the continent to assume office. The delayed independence of South Africa provided Mandela with a unique vantage point to observe the successes and failures of other African leaders over four decades. Mandela read and studied widely throughout his 27-year prison term. He had the opportunity to contemplate, in solitude and together with fellow imprisoned comrades, the state of a nation and continent in crisis. Those reflections, the letters he wrote, and the meetings he held while still in prison refined his philosophy and politics.

His brand of philosophical leadership can be distinguished from that of his African (and global) peers by the absence of ideological purism and the presence of ideological pragmatism. This is his original and philosophical contribution to the world of ideas. Whereas purism leaves no room for the dialectical tensions inherent in human existence, pragmatism navigates gray areas, straddles contradictions, embraces paradoxes, and facilitates synthesis of equal and competing interests.
Arguably, this cultivated in him a range of ideal attributes that the philosopher king should possess:

blockquote.p: For they are lovers of the knowledge of the eternal and of all truth; they are haters of falsehood; their meaner desires are absorbed in the interests of knowledge; they are spectators of all time and all existence. . . . Also they are of a social, gracious disposition, equally free from cowardice and arrogance. They learn and remember easily; they have harmonious, well-regulated minds; truth flows to them sweetly by nature.

div.p: Socrates acknowledges that it would be very rare to find someone who possesses all these qualities. I suggest that Mandela came remarkably close.

He was born into the Xhosa Thembu aristocracy and was destined to succeed his father as a chief but instead traded that role to pursue becoming a lawyer. He later became a leader of ethnic groups beyond his own as the nation’s “Madiba” — his family clan name. Those who met him speak of how he exuded nobility — Socrates’s “social, gracious disposition.” At the same time, he was “equally free from cowardice and arrogance,” as he was both assertive and humble. Giving up his inherited chieftaincy and stepping down after one presidential term distinguished him from African peers who aspired to lifelong presidential power.

As he rose the political leadership ladder, he straddled several ideological positions and tensions. At once, he promoted the African nationalism and socialism that undergirded much of postcolonial Africa and his party, the African National Congress (ANC). He subscribed to communism as a secret member of the South African Communist Party (SACP). He became a patron of the multiracial United Democratic Front (UDF) while an inmate of Pollsmoor Prison in 1983. Ultimately, he presided over the architecture of the new Constitution of the Republic of South Africa (1996), which is acclaimed as a beacon of liberal democracy. Holding all these ideologies cultivated his proficiency in political, social, cultural, and ethical pluralism.

He initially advocated nonviolence when he joined the ANC in the 1940s, then changed his strategy as a founding commander-in-chief of the ANC’s Umkhonto we Sizwe paramilitary wing in the 1960s. During the transition to democracy, he subsequently pivoted definitively to nonviolence. The ability to entertain the continuum of violence from pacifism to radicalism inculcated his discernment of when violence serves a greater purpose and when it is merely gratuitous.

Once he was released from prison, he modeled the surmounting of “meaner desires” such as retribution by championing forgiveness and reconciliation. He became a leader who mediated between victims and villains to bring about a synthesis greater than the interests of either side.

Even though he is sometimes accused of abandoning the more substantive and economic claims of the Freedom Charter of 1955 when he became president, his moral compass was firmly trained on the charter’s preamble: “South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white.” The values of nonracialism and multiculturalism drove his proactive engagement with stakeholders of all races, ethnicities, religions, identities, and interests.

Affectionately known as “Tata” (the isiXhosa term for father), he displayed the kind of unconditional love that a “father” strives to have toward “children” of diverging personalities, different capacities, and competing interests. An apt demonstration of his cultural pluralism was his embrace of rugby (a sport historically dominated by the white minority as players and fans) when South Africa hosted the 1995 Rugby World Cup, and his successful support of the bid to host the 2010 FIFA World Cup in football (a sport dominated by the black majority).

As a revolutionary activist, he made the terrorist lists of many countries, only to be awarded the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize — none of the other African philosopher kings had this privilege. He went on to become a consummate statesman who received more than 250 honors for his life’s work. His name became shorthand for “moral leadership.”

Haig Patapan, in his book Modern Philosopher Kings: Wisdom and Power in Politics (2023), argues that “democracy appears as the most formidable obstacle to all modern attempts to secure philosopher kings.” Yet paradoxically, there is a need for “noble attempts to civilize power and to empower wisdom.” We should bear in mind, though, that while “politics is open to wisdom and philosophy, there are also powerful elements within it resistant to such a union.”
Mandela’s ideological pragmatism intuitively and strategically located the sweet spot where democracy and aristocracy, wisdom and power, philosophy and politics meet.

entry.summary: Although Nelson Mandela lacked the oratory of Nkrumah and the theory of Senghor, his contribution to the world of ideas was something rarer: pragmatism.
